The Mechanism of Thermalization in the Bost–Connes System

Shao-Wu Hu

Shanghai, China · forest@xindong.com

ORCID: 0009-0009-8300-4691

Abstract

Thermalization brings matter toward equilibrium through sustained exchange, while exchange information remains in the joint state. Starting from the dynamical cycle on a finite reduction of the Bost–Connes system, we study the common mechanism underlying thermal equilibrium, relaxation, and local irreversibility. For the cycle constructed here, with independent environment refreshing and same-temperature restoration, we prove that the full Gibbs state is the unique attracting state at fixed finite positive temperature. The occupation spectrum and coherence factors determine observable relaxation rates, and a controlled weak-exchange limit gives continuous relaxation equations on the restored family of states. Thermal exchange and background restoration jointly determine energy changes, yielding conditions for thermal-state tracking and the late-time cooling law of a specified zero-temperature exit process.

Target exchange on complete carriers and an isospectral thermal reference provide a physical realization of this cycle, with a conditional swap and branch pointer implementing background restoration. When the realization preserves the carrier structure, finite switching incorporates maintenance into a driven cycle and control work balances changes in activity energy. If maintenance commutes with shell energy, the same Gibbs state remains attracting, and relaxation is governed by the complete driven-cycle spectrum.

Environment outputs also determine the entropy balance. Decreasing system relative entropy characterizes relaxation, while changes in auxiliary preparations account for environment energy and correlations; restoration auxiliaries may change even at system equilibrium. Reintroducing used auxiliaries can produce returns under the same joint dynamics. Joint tests of occupations, coherences, and energy flows therefore constrain the endpoint, rate, and environmental conditions of thermalization.

Keywords: Bost–Connes system; thermalization; quantum dynamics; relaxation; entropy production; environment records

Contents1. Physical Picture of Thermalization2. Energy Exchange and Thermal Equilibrium3. Relaxation Time Scales4. Cooling and Temperature Evolution5. Irreversibility of Thermalization6. Tests of the Thermalization Mechanism7. ConclusionComputations and DataReferences

1. Physical Picture of Thermalization

Sustained exchange between matter and its environment changes energy occupations and carries distinctions between processes into the environment outputs. In Dynamics of the Bost–Connes State Space [1], we established a complete cycle comprising free evolution, thermal exchange, coherent retrieval, and background restoration. The complete cycle evolves in the joint space of the system and auxiliary units. Taking the partial trace over the auxiliary outputs of the cycle gives the complete system evolution

ℱ(ρ)=Tr⁡ℰ[𝕌tot(ρ⊗ηfull)𝕌tot†].\mathcal F(\rho) =\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathcal E}\!\left[ \mathbb U_{\mathrm{tot}}(\rho\otimes\eta_{\mathrm{full}}) \mathbb U_{\mathrm{tot}}^{\dagger}\right].(1.1)

Here, 𝕌tot\mathbb U_{\mathrm{tot}} is the complete joint action, ηfull\eta_{\mathrm{full}} is the auxiliary preparation for the cycle, and ℰ\mathcal E includes the thermal environment and the auxiliaries responsible for return and restoration. The final system state retains all contributions from matter return, exit, and renewed formation; the auxiliary outputs carry the corresponding energy changes and correlations.

Reference [1] gives conditions under which this cycle preserves the full Gibbs state and brings different initial states toward the same thermal distribution.

1.1 Energy Exchange

Energy exchange in this cycle acts jointly on matter and the environment. Suppose that the system moves from a state of energy EaE_a to one of energy EbE_b, while the corresponding environment energy changes from εin\varepsilon_{\mathrm{in}} to εout\varepsilon_{\mathrm{out}}. An energy-conserving channel satisfies

Eb−Ea=εin−εout.E_b-E_a=\varepsilon_{\mathrm{in}}-\varepsilon_{\mathrm{out}}.(1.2)

The energy gained by the system comes from the environment, and the reverse transfer releases energy to the environment. Allowed exchanges must also satisfy the corresponding charge conservation laws. Their actual amplitudes are determined by the joint matrix elements and interaction durations [1,2]. The same joint action includes both directions. The incoming environment preparation and the channel action together determine their transfer shares in a cycle.

The final joint state generally contains several exchange branches. No exchange, absorption, and emission can correspond to different environment outputs. When the full outputs distinguish these branches, tracing out the environment changes the corresponding system interference. Different energy levels can also produce the same outgoing reading, so whether an exchange distinguishes a particular coherence component must be determined from the actual joint output. Both energy transfer and coherence change follow from this output.

The shell-average background inside the system and the incoming external environment enter the joint state separately. Exiting shares participate in reverse formation after background restoration. The thermal environment carries energy and charge changes, while the restoration auxiliary rearranges the background distribution and retains distinctions between input states. The environment carrier must realize the corresponding joint matrix elements and conservation relations. Auxiliaries involved in coherent retrieval are retained until return is complete; other outputs follow the environmental boundary conditions. The action and energy balance of one cycle determine the starting point of the next [1].

A complete carrier also includes the source and working auxiliaries that maintain its target structure, with previously established correlations retained in the joint state. The system state below describes the target degrees of freedom receiving thermal exchange; sources and spectator degrees of freedom remain in the joint description. Internal thermalization results from exchanges between target modes and background restoration. When maintenance is incorporated into the thermal cycle, the switching work and duration enter the complete balance.

1.2 Evolution of the Distribution

We use the finite reduction RK=ℤ/pKℤR_K=\mathbb Z/p^K\mathbb Z and state space ℋK=ℓ2(RK)\mathcal H_K=\ell^2(R_K), where pp is a fixed odd prime and K≥1K\ge1 is the truncation depth. Shell jj consists of elements of valuation jj, and the terminal shell contains only the zero element. The shell dimensions dj=|Sj|d_j=|S_j| are

dj={(p−1)pK−j−1,0≤j<K,1,j=K,∑j=0Kdj=pK.\begin{gathered} d_j= \begin{cases} (p-1)p^{K-j-1},&0\le j<K,\\ 1,&j=K, \end{cases}\\ \sum_{j=0}^{K}d_j=p^K. \end{gathered}(1.3)

Let ρn\rho_n be the system state after the nnth complete cycle. We use the established thermal-exchange energy HK=∑jEjPjH_K=\sum_j E_jP_j, where PjP_j projects onto shell jj and Ej=jlog⁡pE_j=j\log p. Throughout, ℏ=kB=1\hbar=k_{\mathrm B}=1, and log\log denotes the natural logarithm. Shell occupations and mean energy are

qj(n)=Tr⁡(Pjρn),∑j=0Kqj(n)=1,ES(n)=∑j=0KEjqj(n).\begin{aligned} q_j(n)&=\operatorname{Tr}(P_j\rho_n),\qquad \sum_{j=0}^{K}q_j(n)=1,\\ E_S(n)&=\sum_{j=0}^{K}E_jq_j(n). \end{aligned}(1.4)

The quantity qj(n)q_j(n) is the probability of measuring that energy shell after nn cycles under the same preparation. A shell can still contain different matter modes and their coherences, so shell occupations are only one class of readings of the full state. Shell labels here describe valuation and energy levels; spatial displacement of matter is described by the corresponding position degrees of freedom [2].

With the joint action and environment preparation fixed for all cycles, the complete map ℱ\mathcal F introduced above is applied repeatedly. Each fresh environment and restoration auxiliary is independent of the joint state of the system and all previous environments, and old outputs no longer participate. This description through successive auxiliary units originates in stepwise relaxation models [3] and has been developed in finite-dimensional thermalization models [4] and repeated-interaction theory [5]. Under these conditions,

ρn+1=ℱ(ρn),ρn=ℱn(ρ0).\rho_{n+1}=\mathcal F(\rho_n),\qquad \rho_n=\mathcal F^{\,n}(\rho_0).(1.5)

The same map ℱ\mathcal F acts repeatedly on a changing state. The actual weight of an exchange branch depends on both the channel and the current occupation. A larger occupation of a mode in one cycle changes the total share of exchanges originating from that mode in the next cycle. The combined channel balances change qj(n)q_j(n) and hence the distribution on which subsequent exchanges act.

This iteration retains all branches of return, exit, and renewed formation. Keeping only histories that have never exited would require renormalizing the conditional sample, whose distribution generally differs from that of the full ensemble considered here [1].

1.3 Thermal Equilibrium

A stationary distribution is unchanged by one cycle. To represent thermal equilibrium at inverse temperature β\beta, it must also be compatible with the actual exchange energy. For HKH_K, the Gibbs state on the full space is

ρβ=e−βHKZK,ZK=∑j=0K|Sj|e−βEj.\rho_\beta=\frac{e^{-\beta H_K}}{Z_K},\qquad Z_K=\sum_{j=0}^{K}|S_j|e^{-\beta E_j}.(1.6)

Every independent state at the same energy has the same thermal weight, so the total occupation of that shell is

qjeq=|Sj|e−βEjZK.q_j^{\mathrm{eq}} =\frac{|S_j|e^{-\beta E_j}}{Z_K}.(1.7)

Energy and degeneracy jointly determine the full thermal distribution. A conditional state restricted to the subspace containing one average direction per shell has a partition function computed with the dimensions of those directions. It and the full shell occupations refer to distinct statistical objects.

Forward and reverse exchanges at the same temperature preserve Gibbs weights, and background restoration must be compatible with that temperature as well. If the complete cycle preserves ρβ\rho_\beta, and positive exchange and restoration suffice to remove deviations between initial states, then

ℱ(ρβ)=ρβ,ℱn(ρ0)→ρβ.\mathcal F(\rho_\beta)=\rho_\beta, \qquad \mathcal F^{\,n}(\rho_0)\longrightarrow\rho_\beta.(1.8)

The first relation expresses preservation of the thermal state; the second describes convergence toward it. Together they constitute thermalization [1]. At equilibrium, forward and reverse probability flows are equal in channels satisfying detailed balance, while microscopic exchange can continue. Stationarity of the system distribution does not require every environment auxiliary to remain unchanged.

2. Energy Exchange and Thermal Equilibrium

Energy exchange first changes the states participating in a channel and then, through repeated action, changes the overall occupations. The relative shares of forward and reverse processes are constrained by the environment preparation, while the net flow depends on these shares and the current occupations. For the complete cycle introduced above, choosing propagation stages that do not additionally mix matter modes allows the exchange and occupation balances to be calculated term by term, revealing how thermal equilibrium is established. The energy used throughout is HKH_K; return phases and background restoration belong to the same cycle.

2.1 Exchange between Matter and the Environment

We represent the selected thermal cycle in terms of directional excitations and the shell-average background, decomposing the finite state space orthogonally into the directional excitation space ℳ\mathcal M and the shell-average subspace 𝒞\mathcal C. Hereafter, matter modes are the directional excitations tracked by this cycle; collective matter patterns can also have other representations [2]. Denote these matter modes by |ν⟩|\nu\rangle and the normalized average mode of shell aa by |ea⟩|e_a\rangle. Together they form an orthonormal basis, with projections PνP_\nu and PeaP_{e_a} and energies EνE_\nu and EaE_a, respectively. Allowed exchanges between these modes are supplied by the established joint construction [1].

For a selected channel (a,ν)(a,\nu), the system-side transition operator is

Faν=|ea⟩⟨ν|,[HK,Faν]=(Ea−Eν)Faν.F_{a\nu}=|e_a\rangle\langle\nu|,\qquad [H_K,F_{a\nu}]=(E_a-E_\nu)F_{a\nu}.(2.1)

Write Δaν=Ea−Eν\Delta_{a\nu}=E_a-E_\nu. Assign orthogonal environment states |u⟩,|v⟩|u\rangle,|v\rangle to this channel, with energies and charges that balance at the two joint endpoints. In particular,

Eν+εu=Ea+εv,εu−εv=Δaν.E_\nu+\varepsilon_u=E_a+\varepsilon_v, \qquad \varepsilon_u-\varepsilon_v=\Delta_{a\nu}.(2.2)

Let Laν=Faν⊗|v⟩⟨u|L_{a\nu}=F_{a\nu}\otimes|v\rangle\langle u|. The joint exchange is Waν=exp⁡[αaν(Laν−Laν†)]W_{a\nu}=\exp[\alpha_{a\nu}(L_{a\nu}-L_{a\nu}^{\dagger})], where αaν\alpha_{a\nu} is the actual exchange angle. The generator is anti-Hermitian on the span of the two joint endpoints and vanishes on its orthogonal complement. Its exponential gives

Waν|ν,u⟩=cos⁡αaν|ν,u⟩+sin⁡αaν|ea,v⟩,Waν|ea,v⟩=cos⁡αaν|ea,v⟩−sin⁡αaν|ν,u⟩.\begin{aligned} W_{a\nu}|\nu,u\rangle &=\cos\alpha_{a\nu}|\nu,u\rangle +\sin\alpha_{a\nu}|e_a,v\rangle,\\ W_{a\nu}|e_a,v\rangle &=\cos\alpha_{a\nu}|e_a,v\rangle -\sin\alpha_{a\nu}|\nu,u\rangle. \end{aligned}(2.3)

The first relation gives the branches of matter return and transfer into the background; the second gives background continuation and matter formation. Both transfers have the same exchange angle, and the environment carries the opposite energy and charge changes.

This exchange can be realized on two complete carriers. Let the environment carrier have matching target modes, with FS=|ea⟩⟨ν|F_S=|e_a\rangle\langle\nu| and FB=|ea⟩⟨ν|F_B=|e_a\rangle\langle\nu|. Collect the formation sources, working auxiliaries, and history not participating in exchange into spectator degrees of freedom. The joint exchange generator is

Hex=iΩIsp⊗(FS⊗FB†−FS†⊗FB),[Hex,HK,S+HK,B]=0.\begin{aligned} H_{\mathrm{ex}}&=i\Omega I_{\mathrm{sp}}\otimes (F_S\otimes F_B^\dagger-F_S^\dagger\otimes F_B),\\ [H_{\mathrm{ex}},H_{K,S}+H_{K,B}]&=0. \end{aligned}(2.4)

Here Ω∈ℝ\Omega\in\mathbb R is the exchange strength, and an interaction duration tt gives the exchange angle αaν=Ωt\alpha_{a\nu}=\Omega t. This generates the above rotation between |ν,ea⟩|\nu,e_a\rangle and |ea,ν⟩|e_a,\nu\rangle. Endpoint selection also respects charge conservation, and sources and working auxiliaries are maintained throughout contact. The target can move between directional and shell-average modes while spectator degrees of freedom retain previous correlations. The strict contraction below concerns the reduced target state.

The thermal environment is prepared in tu|u⟩⟨u|+tv|v⟩⟨v|t_u|u\rangle\langle u|+t_v|v\rangle\langle v| within this block. At a common inverse temperature β\beta,

tu=11+eβΔaν,tv=eβΔaν1+eβΔaν,tutv=e−βΔaν.\begin{gathered} t_u=\frac{1}{1+e^{\beta\Delta_{a\nu}}},\qquad t_v=\frac{e^{\beta\Delta_{a\nu}}}{1+e^{\beta\Delta_{a\nu}}},\\ \frac{t_u}{t_v}=e^{-\beta\Delta_{a\nu}}. \end{gathered}(2.5)

Let aaν>0a_{a\nu}>0 be the preparation weight of the selected channel, and retain a weight a0=1−∑a,νaaν>0a_0=1-\sum_{a,\nu}a_{a\nu}>0 for no thermal exchange. Different channels occupy orthogonal environment blocks, whose weights belong to the actual preparation. Squared norms of the exchange branches give the exit and reverse-formation shares in one cycle:

ϵaν=aaνtusin⁡2αaν,fνa=aaνtvsin⁡2αaν.\begin{aligned} \epsilon_{a\nu}&=a_{a\nu}t_u\sin^2\alpha_{a\nu},\\ f_{\nu a}&=a_{a\nu}t_v\sin^2\alpha_{a\nu}. \end{aligned}(2.6)

Every positive exchange channel therefore satisfies

ϵaνfνa=e−β(Ea−Eν).\frac{\epsilon_{a\nu}}{f_{\nu a}} =e^{-\beta(E_a-E_\nu)}.(2.7)

Temperature specifies the ratio of the forward and reverse shares; channel weights and exchange angles set their absolute values. All shares below are counted per cycle. The corresponding mean counting rates require division by the total elapsed duration, including exchange, return, restoration, and the necessary preparation operations.

2.2 Occupation Balance

After exchange, the returning component remains in the matter-mode space, while the background component is restored with fixed shares gag_a. Write

σgsh=∑agaPea,ga>0,∑aga=1.\sigma_g^{\mathrm{sh}}=\sum_a g_aP_{e_a},\qquad g_a>0,\quad\sum_a g_a=1.(2.8)

Coherent retrieval first returns the auxiliary to its initial preparation. The same auxiliary then participates in background restoration, preserving distinctions in the incoming background through orthogonal output labels. After tracing over the full outputs of the thermal environment and this auxiliary, the first-cycle final state of any initial state has the form [1]

ρn=Xn+ynσgsh,n≥1,Xn≥0,Tr⁡Xn+yn=1.\begin{gathered} \rho_n=X_n+y_n\sigma_g^{\mathrm{sh}},\qquad n\ge1,\\ X_n\ge0,\quad\operatorname{Tr}X_n+y_n=1. \end{gathered}(2.9)

Here XnX_n is supported on ℳ\mathcal M and contains both mode occupations and intermode coherences; yny_n is the total background share. Every subsequent cycle preserves this form. If the initial state already has this form, the recursion starts at n=0n=0.

Let xν(n)=⟨ν|Xn|ν⟩x_\nu(n)=\langle\nu|X_n|\nu\rangle. The background endpoint occupation before exchange is yngay_ng_a, so the net exit share of a channel is

Jaν(n)=ϵaνxν(n)−fνaynga.J_{a\nu}(n) =\epsilon_{a\nu}x_\nu(n)-f_{\nu a}y_ng_a.(2.10)

A positive value means net transfer from matter to the background, and a negative value means that reverse formation dominates. The occupations after thermal exchange are

x̃ν=xν−∑aJaν,z̃a=ynga+∑νJaν.\widetilde x_\nu=x_\nu-\sum_aJ_{a\nu},\qquad \widetilde z_a=y_ng_a+\sum_\nu J_{a\nu}.(2.11)

Background restoration preserves the total share ỹ=∑az̃a\widetilde y=\sum_a\widetilde z_a and redistributes it as ỹga\widetilde y g_a. Return phases do not change mode occupations, so a complete cycle obeys

xν(n+1)−xν(n)=−∑aJaν(n),yn+1−yn=∑a,νJaν(n).\begin{aligned} x_\nu(n+1)-x_\nu(n)&=-\sum_aJ_{a\nu}(n),\\ y_{n+1}-y_n&=\sum_{a,\nu}J_{a\nu}(n). \end{aligned}(2.12)

Summing over all channels cancels inflows against outflows and preserves total probability. The updated occupations determine the net flows in the next cycle.

Summing the channels, define ϵν=∑aϵaν\epsilon_\nu=\sum_a\epsilon_{a\nu}, bν(g)=∑agafνab_\nu(g)=\sum_ag_af_{\nu a}, Bg=∑νbν(g)PνB_g=\sum_\nu b_\nu(g)P_\nu, and fΣ=Tr⁡Bgf_\Sigma=\operatorname{Tr}B_g. Denoting the matter-return map by 𝒬\mathcal Q, the full state satisfies the closed recursion

Xn+1=𝒬(Xn)+ynBg,yn+1=Tr⁡[Xn−𝒬(Xn)]+(1−fΣ)yn.\begin{aligned} X_{n+1}&=\mathcal Q(X_n)+y_nB_g,\\ y_{n+1}&=\operatorname{Tr}[X_n-\mathcal Q(X_n)] +(1-f_\Sigma)y_n. \end{aligned}(2.13)

The first term retains returning matter already present, and the second adds matter formed during the current cycle. The occupation equations are the diagonal entries of this matrix recursion; intermode coherences continue to evolve under 𝒬\mathcal Q. Expanding cycle by cycle also separates the original component from those formed in later cycles:

Xn=𝒬n−1(X1)+∑m=1n−1ym𝒬n−1−m(Bg).X_n=\mathcal Q^{\,n-1}(X_1) +\sum_{m=1}^{n-1}y_m\mathcal Q^{\,n-1-m}(B_g).(2.14)

The overall occupation can therefore persist for long times even though each uninterrupted history has a probability of exit.

The same process gives the energy balance. Taking energy gained by the system as positive, thermal exchange and background restoration contribute, respectively,

QT=∑a,ν(Ea−Eν)Jaν,QR=ỹE¯g−∑aEaz̃a,E¯g=∑agaEa.\begin{aligned} Q_T&=\sum_{a,\nu}(E_a-E_\nu)J_{a\nu},\\ Q_R&=\widetilde y\,\overline E_g-\sum_a E_a\widetilde z_a,\\ \overline E_g&=\sum_a g_aE_a. \end{aligned}(2.15)

The first relation follows from the energy difference in each exchange channel, and the second from the background energy change during restoration. The corresponding auxiliaries carry the opposite changes. The auxiliary used for coherent retrieval returns to its preparation at the end of that stage, and the selected propagation also preserves HKH_K. Hence,

ES(n+1)−ES(n)=QT(n)+QR(n).E_S(n+1)-E_S(n)=Q_T(n)+Q_R(n).(2.16)

Energy changes over several cycles are obtained by summing these per-cycle balances. Both whether energy has balanced and whether individual modes are still being redistributed can be tested within the same full state.

2.3 The Thermal Equilibrium Distribution

At stationarity, exit from each matter mode balances formation from the background. If every ϵν>0\epsilon_\nu>0, the occupation equations give

xν*ϵν=y*bν(g).x_\nu^*\epsilon_\nu=y_*b_\nu(g).(2.17)

Using ∑νxν*+y*=1\sum_\nu x_\nu^*+y_*=1 then yields

y*=(1+∑νbν(g)ϵν)−1,xν*=y*bν(g)ϵν.y_*=\left(1+\sum_\nu\frac{b_\nu(g)}{\epsilon_\nu}\right)^{-1}, \qquad x_\nu^*=y_*\frac{b_\nu(g)}{\epsilon_\nu}.(2.18)

These are the stationary occupations of the selected modes. Background restoration enters through bν(g)b_\nu(g). Specifying the forward-to-reverse thermal-exchange ratio alone does not yet specify the endpoint of the complete process.

Choose restoration shares at the same temperature as the thermal environment:

ga=πa=e−βEaZ𝒞,Z𝒞=∑ae−βEa.g_a=\pi_a=\frac{e^{-\beta E_a}}{Z_{\mathcal C}}, \qquad Z_{\mathcal C}=\sum_a e^{-\beta E_a}.(2.19)

The exchange ratio gives, channel by channel,

πafνa=e−βEνZ𝒞ϵaν,bν(π)=e−βEνZ𝒞ϵν.\pi_af_{\nu a} =\frac{e^{-\beta E_\nu}}{Z_{\mathcal C}}\epsilon_{a\nu}, \qquad b_\nu(\pi)=\frac{e^{-\beta E_\nu}}{Z_{\mathcal C}}\epsilon_\nu.(2.20)

The matter and shell-average modes together form a complete orthonormal basis, so

ZK=Z𝒞+∑νe−βEν=∑j|Sj|e−βEj.Z_K =Z_{\mathcal C}+\sum_\nu e^{-\beta E_\nu} =\sum_j|S_j|e^{-\beta E_j}.(2.21)

Substitution into the stationary solution gives

xν*=e−βEνZK,y*=Z𝒞ZK.x_\nu^*=\frac{e^{-\beta E_\nu}}{Z_K}, \qquad y_*=\frac{Z_{\mathcal C}}{Z_K}.(2.22)

These are precisely the diagonal occupations of the full Gibbs state. Since y*πa=e−βEa/ZKy_*\pi_a=e^{-\beta E_a}/Z_K, the channelwise relation also gives Jaν=0J_{a\nu}=0 for every channel. Forward and reverse events still have nonzero shares, but their net contributions cancel.

Invariance of the full state can be checked directly in the joint exchange. In ρβ⊗ηT\rho_\beta\otimes\eta_T, the weights at the two connected endpoints satisfy

aaνZKe−βEνtu=aaνZKe−βEatv.\frac{a_{a\nu}}{Z_K}e^{-\beta E_\nu}t_u =\frac{a_{a\nu}}{Z_K}e^{-\beta E_a}t_v.(2.23)

The joint density operator is proportional to the identity in this two-dimensional subspace and is therefore preserved by the exchange rotation. The environment blocks are mutually orthogonal, and free evolution and return phases also preserve ρβ\rho_\beta. Writing Xβ=∑νe−βEνPν/ZKX_\beta=\sum_\nu e^{-\beta E_\nu}P_\nu/Z_K and yβ=Z𝒞/ZKy_\beta=Z_{\mathcal C}/Z_K, the remaining restoration step gives

ρβ=Xβ+yβσπsh,ℱg(ρβ)=Xβ+yβσgsh.\begin{aligned} \rho_\beta&=X_\beta+y_\beta\sigma_\pi^{\mathrm{sh}},\\ \mathcal F_g(\rho_\beta)&=X_\beta+y_\beta\sigma_g^{\mathrm{sh}}. \end{aligned}(2.24)

At finite temperature, yβ>0y_\beta>0, and the projections PeaP_{e_a} are linearly independent. Therefore,

ℱg(ρβ)=ρβ⇔ga=πafor all a.\mathcal F_g(\rho_\beta)=\rho_\beta \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad g_a=\pi_a\ \text{for all }a.(2.25)

This is the same-temperature equilibrium condition for the selected complete cycle.

2.4 Establishment of Equilibrium

Preservation of the equilibrium distribution by one cycle must be accompanied by convergence from other initial states. Retain the independent environment refreshing conditions of Section 1.2, fix finite β\beta and the restoration preparation, keep a0>0a_0>0, and provide at least one positive exchange channel for each matter mode. Then every ϵν>0\epsilon_\nu>0.

Let ka=1−∑νfνak_a=1-\sum_\nu f_{\nu a} be the share that enters background restoration when starting from background mode eae_a. Since ∑a,νaaν=1−a0\sum_{a,\nu}a_{a\nu}=1-a_0, we have ka≥a0k_a\ge a_0. The total effect associated with entry into restoration in one cycle is

D=∑akaPea+∑νϵνPν,c=min⁡{a0,minνϵν}>0,D≥cI.\begin{gathered} D=\sum_a k_aP_{e_a}+\sum_\nu\epsilon_\nu P_\nu,\\ c=\min\{a_0,\min_\nu\epsilon_\nu\}>0,\qquad D\ge cI. \end{gathered}(2.26)

For any initial state, a share of at least cc enters the same background preparation in each cycle. For an arbitrary input operator AA, subtracting cTr⁡(A)σgshc\operatorname{Tr}(A)\sigma_g^{\mathrm{sh}} from the restoration output leaves a completely positive map: if D=∑iδi|qi⟩⟨qi|D=\sum_i\delta_i|q_i\rangle\langle q_i|, its restoration part has Kraus operators Lai=ga(δi−c)|ea⟩⟨qi|L_{ai}=\sqrt{g_a(\delta_i-c)}|e_a\rangle\langle q_i|. The remaining matter-return component is unchanged, and the remaining total trace is (1−c)Tr⁡A(1-c)\operatorname{Tr}A. Thus the common-restoration decomposition of the complete cycle [1] gives

ℱg(A)=cTr⁡(A)σgsh+(1−c)𝒢g(A),\mathcal F_g(A)=c\operatorname{Tr}(A)\sigma_g^{\mathrm{sh}} +(1-c)\mathcal G_g(A),(2.27)

Here 𝒢g\mathcal G_g is completely positive and trace-preserving. Taking the difference of two normalized states cancels the common background term. Trace-norm contraction of positive trace-preserving maps on self-adjoint operators then gives, cycle by cycle,

∥ℱgn(ρ)−ℱgn(ρ′)∥1≤(1−c)n∥ρ−ρ′∥1.\begin{aligned} &\|\mathcal F_g^{\,n}(\rho)-\mathcal F_g^{\,n}(\rho')\|_1\\ &\qquad\le(1-c)^n\|\rho-\rho'\|_1. \end{aligned}(2.28)

This estimate shows that the complete cycle is a strictly contractive quantum channel [6] and controls both occupation and coherence deviations of the full density operator. Setting ρ′=ρβ\rho'=\rho_\beta, whose invariance has been proved, and g=πg=\pi, we obtain

∥ℱπn(ρ0)−ρβ∥1≤(1−c)n∥ρ0−ρβ∥1→0.\begin{aligned} &\|\mathcal F_\pi^{\,n}(\rho_0)-\rho_\beta\|_1\\ &\qquad\le(1-c)^n\|\rho_0-\rho_\beta\|_1 \longrightarrow0. \end{aligned}(2.29)

Every initial state converges to the same thermal state. If another stationary state existed, substituting it into this estimate would force it to equal ρβ\rho_\beta; the equilibrium state is therefore unique. For general gg, the same contraction also guarantees a unique stationary state: successive state differences decrease as (1−c)n(1-c)^n, their tail sums converge, and the iteration is a Cauchy sequence in the finite-dimensional state space. Thermalization additionally requires the same-temperature preparation condition of the preceding section.

Common restoration in each cycle gradually removes the system’s dependence on its initial state. The joint outputs still preserve the correlations generated by the action, making local equilibration compatible with reversible joint evolution [1]. Quantum homogenization by repeated exchange also demonstrates transfer of initial-state information into joint correlations [7]. Here cc gives a uniform convergence estimate, while particular energy distributions, coherences, and internal labels can decay at different rates. Before calculating these time scales, we specify the physical resources and outputs of same-temperature restoration.

2.5 Physical Realization of Same-Temperature Restoration

Same-temperature restoration can be implemented with a thermal reference isospectral to the shell-average subspace and a branch record. Denote the reference by AA, with input ηA=∑aπa|a⟩⟨a|\eta_A=\sum_a\pi_a|a\rangle\langle a| and energy HA=∑aEa|a⟩⟨a|H_A=\sum_aE_a|a\rangle\langle a|. There is one reference mode per shell, so its weights use Z𝒞Z_{\mathcal C}, not ZKZ_K, which includes all shell degeneracies. Add a zero-energy pointer DD, initially in |0⟩D|0\rangle_D. In the interaction picture, the directional component bypasses the exchange, while the background component swaps with the reference; orthogonal pointer states record the two branches:

V|ν,a,0⟩=wν|ν,a,0⟩,V|eb,a,0⟩=|ea,b,1⟩,|wν|=1.\begin{aligned} V|\nu,a,0\rangle&=w_\nu|\nu,a,0\rangle,\\ V|e_b,a,0\rangle&=|e_a,b,1\rangle, \qquad |w_\nu|=1. \end{aligned}(2.30)

The two sets of inputs and outputs are separately orthogonal and have equal energies term by term, so this action extends to a unitary within each total-energy block. Write P=∑νPνP=\sum_\nu P_\nu, Π=∑aPea\Pi=\sum_aP_{e_a}, and Uw=∑νwνPνU_w=\sum_\nu w_\nu P_\nu. If the new reference and pointer are independent of the target and any previous history OO, tracing out the new outputs gives

(ℛπ⊗Id⁡O)(ρ)=(UwP⊗IO)ρ(PUw†⊗IO)+σπsh⊗Tr⁡S[(Π⊗IO)ρ(Π⊗IO)].\begin{aligned} &(\mathcal R_\pi\otimes\operatorname{Id}_O)(\rho)\\ &=(U_wP\otimes I_O)\rho(PU_w^\dagger\otimes I_O)\\ &\quad+\sigma_\pi^{\mathrm{sh}}\otimes \operatorname{Tr}_S[(\Pi\otimes I_O)\rho(\Pi\otimes I_O)]. \end{aligned}(2.31)

The directional component retains its previous correlations, while the previous background state and its correlations are transferred to the used reference. The pointer removes cross terms between the directional and background components. A controlled swap without a branch record would instead retain πbwν|ν⟩⟨eb|\pi_bw_\nu|\nu\rangle\langle e_b| in the output of |ν⟩⟨eb||\nu\rangle\langle e_b|, and would not realize the displayed map. Isospectral exchange also gives the restoration heat as

QR=ỹE¯π−Tr⁡(HKρ̃𝒞)=−ΔEA,E¯π=∑aπaEa.Q_R=\widetilde y\,\overline E_\pi -\operatorname{Tr}(H_K\widetilde\rho_{\mathcal C}) =-\Delta E_A,\qquad \overline E_\pi=\sum_a\pi_aE_a.(2.32)

Here ρ̃𝒞=Πρ̃Π\widetilde\rho_{\mathcal C}=\Pi\widetilde\rho\Pi and ỹ=Tr⁡ρ̃𝒞\widetilde y=\operatorname{Tr}\widetilde\rho_{\mathcal C}. The reference carries the energy change and the pointer stores branch information; their preparation, loading, and interaction durations enter the complete cycle.

The pure-auxiliary realization of the original cycle can be obtained from the same construction. Introduce a register QQ and physically prepare

|Gπ⟩AQ=∑aπa|a,a⟩,HQ|a⟩=(EK−Ea)|a⟩,R=AQD,|g⟩R=|Gπ⟩AQ|0⟩D.\begin{aligned} |G_\pi\rangle_{AQ}&=\sum_a\sqrt{\pi_a}|a,a\rangle,\\ H_Q|a\rangle&=(E_K-E_a)|a\rangle,\\ R&=AQD,\qquad |g\rangle_R=|G_\pi\rangle_{AQ}|0\rangle_D. \end{aligned}(2.33)

The input has definite total energy EKE_K. The register QQ is a spectator during restoration, and VV still acts only on the target, AA, and DD. Its background branch is

|eb,g⟩↦∑aπa|ea⟩|b,a,1⟩AQD.|e_b,g\rangle\longmapsto \sum_a\sqrt{\pi_a}|e_a\rangle|b,a,1\rangle_{AQD}.(2.34)

Setting |rab⟩=|b,a,1⟩AQD|r_{ab}\rangle=|b,a,1\rangle_{AQD} gives the original orthogonal restoration labels. Tracing out the complete restoration environment RR yields the same ℛπ\mathcal R_\pi, with correlations retained in the joint output. The pure-state realization requires preparation of the whole of AQAQ; the mixed-reference realization has no QQ. Section 5.3 calculates the different environment entropy balances of these two realizations of the same system channel.

3. Relaxation Time Scales

Thermal equilibrium specifies the endpoint of repeated exchange, while relaxation describes how the different deviations from that endpoint decay. In one system, the total matter share, mode composition, and coherence can change at different rates. Other observables may retain information about the initial state even after the mean energy approaches equilibrium. We obtain these time scales from the complete cycle of Chapter 2 [1], using the evolution spectrum to analyze mixing times [8].

In Sections 3.1–3.5, fix the temperature and all cycle data, use same-temperature restoration g=πg=\pi, choose propagation that does not mix matter modes, and retain positive exchange for each mode and a0>0a_0>0. Take 0<αaν<π/20<\alpha_{a\nu}<\pi/2. After one cycle, every initial state enters the closed form ρ=X+yσπsh\rho=X+y\sigma_\pi^{\mathrm{sh}}; these analyses take such a cycle endpoint as the time origin. Denote the total elapsed duration of one cycle by τtot\tau_{\mathrm{tot}}, including exchange, return, restoration, and the required preparation operations. The nnth endpoint is therefore at tn=nτtott_n=n\tau_{\mathrm{tot}}.

3.1 Decay of Occupation Deviations

Retain ϵν=∑aϵaν\epsilon_\nu=\sum_a\epsilon_{a\nu}, bν=∑aπafνab_\nu=\sum_a\pi_af_{\nu a}, and fΣ=∑νbνf_\Sigma=\sum_\nu b_\nu. Let N=dim⁡ℳN=\dim\mathcal M, and arrange matter occupations and the total background share in the column vector v=(x1,…,xN,y)𝖳v=(x_1,\ldots,x_N,y)^{\mathsf T}. The balance equations of Chapter 2 directly give

vn+1=𝖳vn,𝖳=(I−Dϵbϵ𝖳1−fΣ),Dϵ=diag⁡(ϵ1,…,ϵN).\begin{gathered} v_{n+1}=\mathsf T v_n,\qquad \mathsf T= \begin{pmatrix} I-D_\epsilon&b\\ \epsilon^{\mathsf T}&1-f_\Sigma \end{pmatrix},\\ D_\epsilon=\operatorname{diag}(\epsilon_1,\ldots,\epsilon_N). \end{gathered}(3.1)

Each column describes all possible destinations of one initial component. Matter exits with share ϵν\epsilon_\nu and returns with share 1−ϵν1-\epsilon_\nu. The background forms mode ν\nu with share bνb_\nu, while the remainder enters restoration. The equilibrium vector v*v_* satisfies 𝖳v*=v*\mathsf T v_*=v_*, so the deviation δvn=vn−v*\delta v_n=v_n-v_* obeys the same linear evolution.

The equilibrium relation ϵνxν*=bνy*\epsilon_\nu x_\nu^*=b_\nu y_* allows these occupation equations to be symmetrized. Let D*=diag⁡(v*)D_*=\operatorname{diag}(v_*) be the matrix with the equilibrium components on its diagonal. Then

𝖲=D*−1/2𝖳D*1/2=(I−Dϵ𝒉𝒉𝖳1−fΣ),hν=ϵνbν.\begin{gathered} \mathsf S=D_*^{-1/2}\mathsf T D_*^{1/2} =\begin{pmatrix} I-D_\epsilon&\boldsymbol h\\ \boldsymbol h^{\mathsf T}&1-f_\Sigma \end{pmatrix},\\ h_\nu=\sqrt{\epsilon_\nu b_\nu}. \end{gathered}(3.2)

Both exit and formation shares enter the eigenvalues. Let 𝒆ν\mathbf e_\nu and 𝒆y\mathbf e_y denote the coordinate basis of occupation vectors, and define ℓν=ϵν𝒆ν−bν𝒆y\ell_\nu=\sqrt{\epsilon_\nu}\mathbf e_\nu-\sqrt{b_\nu}\mathbf e_y. We have

I−𝖲=∑νℓνℓν𝖳≥0,Tr⁡(I−𝖲)=∑νϵν+fΣ≤∑a,ν(ϵaν+fνa)≤1−a0.\begin{aligned} I-\mathsf S&=\sum_\nu \ell_\nu \ell_\nu^{\mathsf T}\ge0,\\ \operatorname{Tr}(I-\mathsf S) &=\sum_\nu\epsilon_\nu+f_\Sigma\\ &\le\sum_{a,\nu}(\epsilon_{a\nu}+f_{\nu a}) \le1-a_0. \end{aligned}(3.3)

All eigenvalues are therefore real and lie in [a0,1][a_0,1]. Since every mode is connected to the background, eigenvalue 11 occurs only along the normalized equilibrium direction; all other eigenvalues satisfy a0≤λr<1a_0\le\lambda_r<1. Each occupation mode decays cycle by cycle, although individual occupations formed by superposing several modes can still vary nonmonotonically. For general parameters, all are determined by the same finite matrix, whose characteristic polynomial is

det⁡(λI−𝖳)=(λ−1+fΣ)∏ν(λ−1+ϵν)−∑νϵνbν∏μ≠ν(λ−1+ϵμ).\begin{aligned} &\det(\lambda I-\mathsf T)\\ &=(\lambda-1+f_\Sigma) \prod_\nu(\lambda-1+\epsilon_\nu)\\ &\quad-\sum_\nu\epsilon_\nu b_\nu \prod_{\mu\ne\nu}(\lambda-1+\epsilon_\mu). \end{aligned}(3.4)

This follows by eliminating the diagonal matter block against the background row. Written as a polynomial, it also includes repeated roots when different exit shares coincide.

Choose orthonormal eigenvectors uru_r of 𝖲\mathsf S, with u0=v*u_0=\sqrt{v_*} corresponding to equilibrium. Normalization makes the weighted deviation D*−1/2δv0D_*^{-1/2}\delta v_0 orthogonal to that direction. Hence,

δvn=D*1/2∑r=1NArλrnur,Ar=ur𝖳D*−1/2δv0.\begin{aligned} \delta v_n&=D_*^{1/2}\sum_{r=1}^{N} A_r\lambda_r^n u_r,\\ A_r&=u_r^{\mathsf T}D_*^{-1/2}\delta v_0. \end{aligned}(3.5)

Each weighted vector D*1/2urD_*^{1/2}u_r specifies a coordinated change of occupations: some matter modes increase while other modes or the background decrease, preserving total probability. This combination is multiplied by λr\lambda_r in every cycle. Expressed using the same total elapsed duration,

λrn=e−Γrtn,Γr=−log⁡λrτtot,τr=Γr−1.\begin{gathered} \lambda_r^n=e^{-\Gamma_r t_n},\qquad \Gamma_r=-\frac{\log\lambda_r}{\tau_{\mathrm{tot}}},\\ \tau_r=\Gamma_r^{-1}. \end{gathered}(3.6)

The quantity τr\tau_r is the exponential time scale over which this component falls to e−1e^{-1} of its initial amplitude. These relations describe cycle endpoints exactly. Only when 1−λr≪11-\lambda_r\ll1 can one use Γr≃(1−λr)/τtot\Gamma_r\simeq(1-\lambda_r)/\tau_{\mathrm{tot}}. A single-exchange counting share, a per-cycle decay factor, and a relaxation rate per unit time are thus separately specified.

3.2 Energy and Mode Composition

Mean energy probes only part of the occupation deviation. Number the matter modes as ν1,…,νN\nu_1,\ldots,\nu_N, and let E¯π=∑aπaEa\overline E_\pi=\sum_a\pi_aE_a be the mean background energy. Arrange the component energies in the column vector e=(Eν1,…,EνN,E¯π)𝖳e=(E_{\nu_1},\ldots,E_{\nu_N},\overline E_\pi)^{\mathsf T}. Substitution into the preceding expansion yields

ES(n)−ES*=e𝖳δvn=∑r=1NAr(e𝖳D*1/2ur)λrn.\begin{aligned} E_S(n)-E_S^* &=e^{\mathsf T}\delta v_n\\ &=\sum_{r=1}^{N} A_r\bigl(e^{\mathsf T}D_*^{1/2}u_r\bigr)\lambda_r^n. \end{aligned}(3.7)

For a slow mode to appear in the energy curve, it must be excited by the initial state and have a nonzero energy response. When occupations are redistributed among modes of equal energy, the mean energy can remain unchanged even though their detection probabilities continue to vary. Verifying complete thermalization therefore also requires examining these internal occupations.

This distinction can be solved exactly when N≥2N\ge2 and all matter modes have the same exit share ϵν=ϵ>0\epsilon_\nu=\epsilon>0. The background equation reduces to

yn+1=ϵ+(1−ϵ−fΣ)yn,y*=ϵϵ+fΣ,yn−y*=(1−ϵ−fΣ)n(y0−y*).\begin{aligned} y_{n+1}&=\epsilon+(1-\epsilon-f_\Sigma)y_n,\\ y_*&=\frac{\epsilon}{\epsilon+f_\Sigma},\\ y_n-y_*&=(1-\epsilon-f_\Sigma)^n(y_0-y_*). \end{aligned}(3.8)

The total matter share 1−yn1-y_n approaches equilibrium at the same rate. Now let rν=bν/fΣr_\nu=b_\nu/f_\Sigma, and define deviations of the internal matter occupations by

zν(n)=xν(n)−rν(1−yn),∑νzν(n)=0.\begin{gathered} z_\nu(n)=x_\nu(n)-r_\nu(1-y_n),\\ \sum_\nu z_\nu(n)=0. \end{gathered}(3.9)

Substitute xν(n+1)=(1−ϵ)xν(n)+bνynx_\nu(n+1)=(1-\epsilon)x_\nu(n)+b_\nu y_n and the background equation. Using rνfΣ=bνr_\nu f_\Sigma=b_\nu, all formation terms cancel, leaving

zν(n)=(1−ϵ)nzν(0),xν(n)=rν(1−yn)+(1−ϵ)nzν(0).\begin{aligned} z_\nu(n)&=(1-\epsilon)^n z_\nu(0),\\ x_\nu(n)&=r_\nu(1-y_n)+(1-\epsilon)^n z_\nu(0). \end{aligned}(3.10)

The total share and internal composition thus have two different decay factors:

λtot=1−ϵ−fΣ,Γtot=−log⁡λtotτtot,λcomp=1−ϵ,Γcomp=−log⁡λcompτtot.\begin{aligned} \lambda_{\mathrm{tot}}&=1-\epsilon-f_\Sigma, &\Gamma_{\mathrm{tot}}&=-\frac{\log\lambda_{\mathrm{tot}}}{\tau_{\mathrm{tot}}},\\ \lambda_{\mathrm{comp}}&=1-\epsilon, &\Gamma_{\mathrm{comp}}&=-\frac{\log\lambda_{\mathrm{comp}}}{\tau_{\mathrm{tot}}}. \end{aligned}(3.11)

The internal composition has N−1N-1 independent components. Since fΣ>0f_\Sigma>0, we have Γtot>Γcomp\Gamma_{\mathrm{tot}}>\Gamma_{\mathrm{comp}}: the total matter and background shares balance more rapidly, while the relative occupations of matter modes can continue to adjust. This rate difference is already contained in the same exit and formation shares.

Writing Eℳ=∑νrνEνE_{\mathcal M}=\sum_\nu r_\nu E_\nu, the corresponding energy curve is

ES(n)−ES*=(E¯π−Eℳ)(y0−y*)λtotn+λcompn∑νEνzν(0).\begin{aligned} E_S(n)-E_S^* &=(\overline E_\pi-E_{\mathcal M})(y_0-y_*) \lambda_{\mathrm{tot}}^n\\ &\quad+\lambda_{\mathrm{comp}}^n \sum_\nu E_\nu z_\nu(0). \end{aligned}(3.12)

If these matter modes have equal energies, the second term vanishes because ∑νzν=0\sum_\nu z_\nu=0. The energy curve then shows only the faster relaxation of the total share, while measurements of internal modes still reveal the slower composition change.

3.3 Coherence Decay

Coherences between matter modes evolve through the same cycle. Thermal exchange changes each mode’s return amplitude, and the full environment output retains differences between these amplitudes. Tracing out the environment then changes the off-diagonal entries. Background restoration produces only the shell-average component, and renewed formation adds only diagonal matter occupations. Neither supplies coherence between different matter modes [1].

Let Daλ=Iℳ+(cos⁡αaλ−1)PλD_{a\lambda}=I_{\mathcal M}+(\cos\alpha_{a\lambda}-1)P_\lambda be the diagonal return operator for channel (a,λ)(a,\lambda). For environment input uu, it gives the matter-return amplitude; for input vv, the existing matter component is preserved. Denote the net cycle phase from free evolution and coherent retrieval by φν\varphi_\nu. Its action on the matter space is Uφ=∑νeiφνPνU_\varphi=\sum_\nu e^{i\varphi_\nu}P_\nu. With this phase removed, the complete return map is

Uφ†𝒬(X)Uφ=a0X+∑a,λaaλ[tuDaλXDaλ+tvX].\begin{aligned} &U_\varphi^\dagger\mathcal Q(X)U_\varphi\\ &=a_0X+\sum_{a,\lambda}a_{a\lambda} \bigl[t_uD_{a\lambda}XD_{a\lambda}+t_vX\bigr]. \end{aligned}(3.13)

For ν≠μ\nu\ne\mu, a channel changes at most one side of |ν⟩⟨μ||\nu\rangle\langle\mu|. Summing channel contributions and defining

dν=∑aaaνtu(1−cos⁡αaν),γνμ=1−dν−dμ,\begin{aligned} d_\nu&=\sum_a a_{a\nu}t_u(1-\cos\alpha_{a\nu}),\\ \gamma_{\nu\mu}&=1-d_\nu-d_\mu, \end{aligned}(3.14)

gives the exact coherence factor of the complete cycle and its iteration:

ℱ(|ν⟩⟨μ|)=γνμei(φν−φμ)|ν⟩⟨μ|,ρνμ(n)=γνμnein(φν−φμ)ρνμ(0).\begin{aligned} \mathcal F(|\nu\rangle\langle\mu|) &=\gamma_{\nu\mu}e^{i(\varphi_\nu-\varphi_\mu)} |\nu\rangle\langle\mu|,\\ \rho_{\nu\mu}(n) &=\gamma_{\nu\mu}^{\,n} e^{in(\varphi_\nu-\varphi_\mu)}\rho_{\nu\mu}(0). \end{aligned}(3.15)

The chosen exchange angles and positive channel weights ensure a0≤γνμ<1a_0\le\gamma_{\nu\mu}<1. The magnitude of the off-diagonal entry decays at the rate

Γνμcoh=−log⁡γνμτtot\Gamma_{\nu\mu}^{\mathrm{coh}} =-\frac{\log\gamma_{\nu\mu}}{\tau_{\mathrm{tot}}}(3.16)

while the difference in net cycle phases makes interference readings oscillate from one cycle to the next. For example, the expectation of Aνμ=|μ⟩⟨ν|+|ν⟩⟨μ|A_{\nu\mu}=|\mu\rangle\langle\nu|+|\nu\rangle\langle\mu| is

⟨Aνμ⟩n=2γνμnRe⁡[ein(φν−φμ)ρνμ(0)].\langle A_{\nu\mu}\rangle_n =2\gamma_{\nu\mu}^{\,n} \operatorname{Re}\!\left[ e^{in(\varphi_\nu-\varphi_\mu)}\rho_{\nu\mu}(0)\right].(3.17)

Coherence decay therefore appears as a change in the envelope of an actual interference signal. This signal and the energy curve read off-diagonal and diagonal components of the same full state. The different constraints on coherence and occupations in thermal processes can also be analyzed through time-translation symmetry [9].

Exchange shares and return amplitudes yield a direct comparison. Applying sin⁡2α=(1−cos⁡α)(1+cos⁡α)\sin^2\alpha=(1-\cos\alpha)(1+\cos\alpha) channel by channel gives

dν=∑aϵaν1+cos⁡αaν,ϵν2<dν<ϵν.d_\nu=\sum_a\frac{\epsilon_{a\nu}}{1+\cos\alpha_{a\nu}}, \qquad \frac{\epsilon_\nu}{2}<d_\nu<\epsilon_\nu.(3.18)

For the equal exit shares of the preceding section, γνμ<1−ϵ\gamma_{\nu\mu}<1-\epsilon, so coherence decays faster than the internal composition. Its ordering relative to total-share relaxation still depends on the comparison between dν+dμd_\nu+d_\mu and ϵ+fΣ\epsilon+f_\Sigma. For unequal exit shares, one must calculate the occupation spectrum and coherence factors separately before comparing the time scales of actual readings.

3.4 Continuous Relaxation under Weak Exchange

When exchange per cycle is sufficiently weak, many complete cycles accumulate into continuous changes in occupations and coherences. Continuous limits of repeated interactions and their weak-coupling time scales have been studied rigorously [10,11]. Keep all other cycle data fixed and set only the exchange angles to αaν(h)=hθaν\alpha_{a\nu}(h)=\sqrt h\,\theta_{a\nu}, where h>0h>0 is dimensionless and θaν\theta_{a\nu} is fixed. Starting from a fixed state X0+y0σπshX_0+y_0\sigma_\pi^{\mathrm{sh}} in the closed family, remove the accumulated diagonal phase at the endpoints: X̃n=Uφ−nXnUφn\widetilde X_n=U_\varphi^{-n}X_nU_\varphi^n. Return, exit, and diagonal formation are compatible with this transformation, and tildes are omitted below. Introduce slow time and two sets of rates:

sn=htn=hnτtot,κνout=1τtot∑aaaνtu(aν)θaν2,κνin=1τtot∑aπaaaνtv(aν)θaν2.\begin{aligned} s_n&=ht_n=hn\tau_{\mathrm{tot}},\\ \kappa_\nu^{\mathrm{out}} &=\frac{1}{\tau_{\mathrm{tot}}} \sum_a a_{a\nu}t_u^{(a\nu)}\theta_{a\nu}^{\,2},\\ \kappa_\nu^{\mathrm{in}} &=\frac{1}{\tau_{\mathrm{tot}}} \sum_a\pi_a a_{a\nu}t_v^{(a\nu)}\theta_{a\nu}^{\,2}. \end{aligned}(3.19)

The expansions sin⁡2(hθ)=hθ2+O(h2)\sin^2(\sqrt h\,\theta)=h\theta^2+O(h^2) and 1−cos⁡(hθ)=hθ2/2+O(h2)1-\cos(\sqrt h\,\theta)=h\theta^2/2+O(h^2) give the per-cycle shares and coherence losses as

ϵν(h)=hτtotκνout+O(h2),bν(h)=hτtotκνin+O(h2),dν(h)=12hτtotκνout+O(h2).\begin{aligned} \epsilon_\nu(h)&=h\tau_{\mathrm{tot}}\kappa_\nu^{\mathrm{out}}+O(h^2),\\ b_\nu(h)&=h\tau_{\mathrm{tot}}\kappa_\nu^{\mathrm{in}}+O(h^2),\\ d_\nu(h)&=\tfrac12h\tau_{\mathrm{tot}}\kappa_\nu^{\mathrm{out}}+O(h^2). \end{aligned}(3.20)

The finite number of fixed channels makes the remainders uniformly controlled. Write 𝖪out=∑νκνoutPν\mathsf K_{\mathrm{out}}=\sum_\nu\kappa_\nu^{\mathrm{out}}P_\nu, 𝖪in=∑νκνinPν\mathsf K_{\mathrm{in}}=\sum_\nu\kappa_\nu^{\mathrm{in}}P_\nu, and κΣin=∑νκνin\kappa_\Sigma^{\mathrm{in}}=\sum_\nu\kappa_\nu^{\mathrm{in}}. Substituting into the exact occupation and off-diagonal recursions and dividing successive endpoint differences by hτtoth\tau_{\mathrm{tot}} gives the slow-time equations

dXds=−12{𝖪out,X}+y𝖪in,dyds=Tr⁡(𝖪outX)−κΣiny.\begin{aligned} \frac{dX}{ds} &=-\tfrac12\{\mathsf K_{\mathrm{out}},X\} +y\mathsf K_{\mathrm{in}},\\ \frac{dy}{ds} &=\operatorname{Tr}(\mathsf K_{\mathrm{out}}X) -\kappa_\Sigma^{\mathrm{in}}y. \end{aligned}(3.21)

Exit reduces the existing matter component, and reverse formation adds diagonal occupations. Their contributions to the total background share have the opposite signs. Off-diagonal entries satisfy dXνμ/ds=−(κνout+κμout)Xνμ/2dX_{\nu\mu}/ds=-(\kappa_\nu^{\mathrm{out}}+\kappa_\mu^{\mathrm{out}})X_{\nu\mu}/2, so their decay is determined by the same exit rates.

These equations have an explicit completely positive evolution representation. Use a mathematical label |⋆⟩|\star\rangle to encode the total background share, write ρ̂=X⊕y\widehat\rho=X\oplus y on ℋ̂=ℳ⊕ℂ|⋆⟩\widehat{\mathcal H}=\mathcal M\oplus\mathbb C|\star\rangle, and set

Jνout=κνout|⋆⟩⟨ν|,Jνin=κνin|ν⟩⟨⋆|,𝒟[J](A)=JAJ†−12{J†J,A},ℒ=∑ν(𝒟[Jνout]+𝒟[Jνin]).\begin{aligned} J_\nu^{\mathrm{out}}&=\sqrt{\kappa_\nu^{\mathrm{out}}} |\star\rangle\langle\nu|,\\ J_\nu^{\mathrm{in}}&=\sqrt{\kappa_\nu^{\mathrm{in}}} |\nu\rangle\langle\star|,\\ \mathcal D[J](A)&=JAJ^\dagger-\tfrac12\{J^\dagger J,A\},\\ \mathcal L&=\sum_\nu\bigl(\mathcal D[J_\nu^{\mathrm{out}}] +\mathcal D[J_\nu^{\mathrm{in}}]\bigr). \end{aligned}(3.22)

This Gorini–Kossakowski–Sudarshan–Lindblad (GKSL) generator [12,13] gives exactly the preceding equations on block-diagonal states ρ̂\widehat\rho. The label |⋆⟩|\star\rangle encodes only the total share. The physical background remains the distribution σπsh\sigma_\pi^{\mathrm{sh}}, rather than becoming a single energy level. The same-temperature relation gives, channel by channel,

κνinκνout=e−βEνZ𝒞,xν*=e−βEνZK,y*=Z𝒞ZK.\frac{\kappa_\nu^{\mathrm{in}}}{\kappa_\nu^{\mathrm{out}}} =\frac{e^{-\beta E_\nu}}{Z_{\mathcal C}}, \qquad x_\nu^*=\frac{e^{-\beta E_\nu}}{Z_K},\quad y_*=\frac{Z_{\mathcal C}}{Z_K}.(3.23)

If every mode has at least one channel with θaν>0\theta_{a\nu}>0, exit rates are positive, the occupation chain is connected, and coherences decay. The limiting equations therefore still converge to the same full thermal state.

Let Φh\Phi_h be the single-cycle map after phase removal and encoding, restricted to the above block-diagonal operator space. Expanding the finite-dimensional cycle map and the semigroup exponential gives ∥Φh−ehτtotℒ∥1→1,sa≤C0h2\|\Phi_h-e^{h\tau_{\mathrm{tot}}\mathcal L}\|_{1\to1,\mathrm{sa}}\le C_0h^2, where the norm acts on self-adjoint operators in that space. Both evolutions preserve this space and contract the trace norm on its self-adjoint operators. Subtracting successive iterates and using a telescoping sum yields

∥Φhn(ρ̂0)−esnℒρ̂0∥1≤nC0h2≤C0Sτtoth,0≤sn≤S.\begin{aligned} &\|\Phi_h^{\,n}(\widehat\rho_0) -e^{s_n\mathcal L}\widehat\rho_0\|_1\\ &\qquad\le nC_0h^2 \le\frac{C_0S}{\tau_{\mathrm{tot}}}h, \qquad 0\le s_n\le S. \end{aligned}(3.24)

This proves uniform convergence on every fixed finite slow-time interval after removal of the net cycle phase. Taking n=⌊s/(hτtot)⌋n=\lfloor s/(h\tau_{\mathrm{tot}})\rfloor leaves less than one cycle of slow time, adding only an O(h)O(h) error. Reconstructing both states as X+yσπshX+y\sigma_\pi^{\mathrm{sh}} and restoring the accumulated phase UφnU_\varphi^n to both matter blocks preserve the trace norm of their difference. The same error bound therefore holds when comparing the original physical state with the corresponding rotating reference state.

Weak exchange does not shorten the total elapsed duration of return and restoration. Let PℳP_{\mathcal M} and P𝒞P_{\mathcal C} project onto the two subspaces, extend the net cycle phase action as Ûφ=P𝒞+Uφ\widehat U_\varphi=P_{\mathcal C}+U_\varphi, and write 𝒰φ(A)=ÛφAÛφ†\mathcal U_\varphi(A)=\widehat U_\varphi A\widehat U_\varphi^\dagger. The single-cycle limit on the full space is then

ℱh→𝒰φ∘ℰπ,ℰπ(A)=PℳAPℳ+Tr⁡(P𝒞A)σπsh.\begin{aligned} \mathcal F_h&\longrightarrow\mathcal U_\varphi\circ\mathcal E_\pi,\\ \mathcal E_\pi(A)&=P_{\mathcal M}AP_{\mathcal M} +\operatorname{Tr}(P_{\mathcal C}A)\sigma_\pi^{\mathrm{sh}}. \end{aligned}(3.25)

Background restoration remains after phase removal. This limit is the identity only on the restored closed family of states. The continuous equations thus describe slow changes accumulated over many weak-exchange cycles. The coherence decay rate in the original physical time is correspondingly

Γνμcoh(h)=hκνout+κμout2+O(h2).\Gamma_{\nu\mu}^{\mathrm{coh}}(h) =h\,\frac{\kappa_\nu^{\mathrm{out}}+\kappa_\mu^{\mathrm{out}}}{2} +O(h^2).(3.26)

3.5 Slow Modes and Thermalization Time

Return to the complete cycle with fixed exchange angles and physical time tn=nτtott_n=n\tau_{\mathrm{tot}}. After the first restoration, state deviations consist of occupation and coherence modes. Long-time readings are controlled by the slowest component that is both excited by the initial state and accessible to the observable.

Including all modes, define

rslow=max⁡{maxr≥1λr,maxν≠μγνμ}<1,Γslow=−log⁡rslowτtot.\begin{gathered} r_{\mathrm{slow}}= \max\!\left\{\max_{r\ge1}\lambda_r, \max_{\nu\ne\mu}\gamma_{\nu\mu}\right\}<1,\\ \Gamma_{\mathrm{slow}} =-\frac{\log r_{\mathrm{slow}}}{\tau_{\mathrm{tot}}}. \end{gathered}(3.27)

If there is only one matter mode, the coherence term is absent. The common-restoration lower bound in Chapter 2 also ensures

rslow≤1−c,Γslow≥−log⁡(1−c)τtot.r_{\mathrm{slow}}\le1-c,\qquad \Gamma_{\mathrm{slow}}\ge -\frac{\log(1-c)}{\tau_{\mathrm{tot}}}.(3.28)

This uniform estimate guarantees decay of deviations, while the actual thermalization rate is determined by the calculated spectrum. If the late-time envelope of a reading is dominated by CAe−ΓAtnC_Ae^{-\Gamma_A t_n}, the time needed to reach error δ\delta is approximately

tδ≃1ΓAlog⁡|CA|δ,t_\delta\simeq\frac{1}{\Gamma_A} \log\frac{|C_A|}{\delta},(3.29)

The actual endpoint is the first complete-cycle count no earlier than this time. Greater precision resolves slow components previously obscured by faster processes.

When mode rates are well separated, energy readings may already have stabilized while the internal composition still retains information about the initial preparation. Spectral separation of time scales also underlies metastability in open quantum dynamics [14]. Let Γf\Gamma_{\mathrm f} and Γs\Gamma_{\mathrm s} be the envelope decay rates of selected fast and slow modes. In units of their respective initial amplitudes, requiring the fast mode to fall below δ\delta and the slow mode to change by no more than δ\delta, with 0<δ<10<\delta<1, gives e−Γftn≤δe^{-\Gamma_{\mathrm f}t_n}\le\delta and 1−e−Γstn≤δ1-e^{-\Gamma_{\mathrm s}t_n}\le\delta. Both conditions hold in the time window

log⁡(1/δ)Γf≤tn≤−log⁡(1−δ)Γs.\frac{\log(1/\delta)}{\Gamma_{\mathrm f}} \le t_n\le \frac{-\log(1-\delta)}{\Gamma_{\mathrm s}}.(3.30)

This interval must contain an actual cycle endpoint. Readings that superpose several modes also require the actual amplitudes of all excited modes to be included.

How long a slow component persists also depends on the energy exchange needed to change it. If exit requires absorption of energy from the environment, cooling reduces the opportunities for such exchange. Again consider the case N≥2N\ge2 with the same exit share for all matter modes. Let each matter mode exchange only with a background endpoint one shell higher, so the established shell spectrum gives Δ=Ea−Eν=log⁡p\Delta=E_a-E_\nu=\log p. Assign the same weight aexa_{\mathrm{ex}} and exchange angle α\alpha to every channel, with Naex<1Na_{\mathrm{ex}}<1. Then

ϵ=aexsin⁡2α1+eβΔ,Γcomp=−log⁡(1−ϵ)τtot.\epsilon=\frac{a_{\mathrm{ex}}\sin^2\alpha}{1+e^{\beta\Delta}}, \qquad \Gamma_{\mathrm{comp}}=-\frac{\log(1-\epsilon)}{\tau_{\mathrm{tot}}}.(3.31)

For βΔ≫1\beta\Delta\gg1, with weights, exchange angles, and total elapsed duration fixed,

Γcomp∼aexsin⁡2ατtote−βΔ.\Gamma_{\mathrm{comp}} \sim\frac{a_{\mathrm{ex}}\sin^2\alpha}{\tau_{\mathrm{tot}}} e^{-\beta\Delta}.(3.32)

The activation energy is the energy Δ\Delta that the exit channel actually needs to absorb. Additional exit channels that require no energy increase can remove this exponential slowing. When several channels coexist, all must be included in the occupation matrix. The same structure can therefore ultimately thermalize at finite temperature while the relative matter-mode occupations retain information about the initial preparation for long but finite observation times.

3.6 Thermalization during Maintenance

We now consider internal thermalization of a stationary carrier during maintenance. Let the target maintenance generator MM satisfy [HK,M]=0[H_K,M]=0. Each cycle consists of maintenance evolution, finite-time switch-off, thermal exchange and restoration, and finite-time switch-on. Let 𝒥\mathcal J embed the target into the complete carrier. The joint evolution is required to preserve this encoded subspace, retaining formation sources and working auxiliaries throughout. The corresponding intertwining relations are

Ĥ(s)𝒥=𝒥(HK+sM+EωI),V̂(𝒥⊗Iℰ)=(𝒥⊗Iℰ)V.\begin{aligned} \widehat H(s)\mathcal J &=\mathcal J(H_K+sM+E_\omega I),\\ \widehat V(\mathcal J\otimes I_{\mathcal E}) &=(\mathcal J\otimes I_{\mathcal E})V. \end{aligned}(3.33)

Here ss is the switching envelope, EωE_\omega is the fixed energy contribution of the source and spectator degrees of freedom, and VV acts jointly on the target and thermal-cycle auxiliaries. If the unprotected joint generator does not preserve this subspace, the apparatus must provide protection or compensation throughout switching and thermal exchange.

Let maintenance last tHt_H, with linear switch-off and switch-on durations t↓,t↑t_{\downarrow},t_{\uparrow}. In the interaction picture of HKH_K, the maintenance evolutions before and after the thermal cycle are

U−=e−ib−M,b−=tH+t↓/2,U+=e−ib+M,b+=t↑/2.\begin{aligned} U_-&=e^{-ib_-M},& b_-&=t_H+t_{\downarrow}/2,\\ U_+&=e^{-ib_+M},& b_+&=t_{\uparrow}/2. \end{aligned}(3.34)

For other switching envelopes, the corresponding integrals replace the half-areas. During the pause, perform the thermal exchange, coherent retrieval, and same-temperature restoration of Chapter 2, with return phase wν=1w_\nu=1. Denoting the thermal-cycle channel with the free shell phase removed by ℱπ(0)\mathcal F_\pi^{(0)}, the complete driven cycle is

ℱdrv=Ad⁡e−iHKτdrvU+∘ℱπ(0)∘Ad⁡U−.\mathcal F_{\mathrm{drv}} =\operatorname{Ad}_{e^{-iH_K\tau_{\mathrm{drv}}}U_+} \circ\mathcal F_\pi^{(0)}\circ\operatorname{Ad}_{U_-}.(3.35)

Here Ad⁡U(ρ)=UρU†\operatorname{Ad}_U(\rho)=U\rho U^\dagger, and the total elapsed duration τdrv\tau_{\mathrm{drv}} includes maintenance, switching, thermal contact, retrieval, restoration, recording, loading, and routing. The free shell phase is included in the final factor, while ℱπ(0)\mathcal F_\pi^{(0)} describes the thermal cycle in the interaction picture.

The same evolution determines the control work during switching. Set ρ−=U−ρU−†\rho_-=U_-\rho U_-^\dagger and σ=ℱπ(0)(ρ−)\sigma=\mathcal F_\pi^{(0)}(\rho_-). Each switching stage preserves the expectation of MM, so the work delivered by the controller to the target is

Wctrl=−Tr⁡(Mρ−)+Tr⁡(Mσ).W_{\mathrm{ctrl}} =-\operatorname{Tr}(M\rho_-)+\operatorname{Tr}(M\sigma).(3.36)

The two terms follow from integrating ∫ṡ⟨M⟩dt\int\dot s\langle M\rangle\,dt over switch-off and switch-on. Their sum is determined by the change in maintenance energy across the thermal cycle. Choose endpoints with system activity on at the start and end of the cycle, while the target activity of environment carrier BB remains paused during supply, contact, and storage after use. With sources and formation auxiliaries retained by the stated protection,

ΔES(HK+M)+ΔEB(HK)+ΔER=Wctrl.\begin{aligned} \Delta E_S(H_K+M)+\Delta E_B(H_K) +\Delta E_R=W_{\mathrm{ctrl}}. \end{aligned}(3.37)

The thermal reference carries the energy change of restoration environment RR, while the spectator register is unchanged. Reactivating the used environment carrier requires its own control work; initial preparation and continuous protection also enter the apparatus-level resource balance.

Since [HK,M]=0[H_K,M]=0, both surrounding unitaries preserve ρβ=e−βHK/ZK\rho_\beta=e^{-\beta H_K}/Z_K. The thermal-cycle channel preserves the same thermal state and inherits the common-restoration decomposition of Section 2.4. The complete driven cycle therefore preserves ρβ\rho_\beta as well, and any two target states obey

ℱdrv(ρβ)=ρβ,∥ℱdrvn(ρ)−ℱdrvn(ρ′)∥1≤(1−c)n∥ρ−ρ′∥1.\begin{aligned} \mathcal F_{\mathrm{drv}}(\rho_\beta)&=\rho_\beta,\\ \|\mathcal F_{\mathrm{drv}}^{\,n}(\rho) -\mathcal F_{\mathrm{drv}}^{\,n}(\rho')\|_1 &\le(1-c)^n\|\rho-\rho'\|_1. \end{aligned}(3.38)

The surrounding unitaries preserve the trace norm. Applying the original contraction bound to the intervening thermal cycle and iterating gives the displayed estimate and the unique attracting state. Section 6.4 describes implementation with a finite independent resource supply. This equilibrium is determined by shell energy HKH_K and the driven protocol; Gibbs equilibrium for the endpoint total energy HK+MH_K+M is a separate question.

Maintenance generally mixes directional occupations and coherences, so relaxation must be recalculated from the spectrum of the full ℱdrv\mathcal F_{\mathrm{drv}}. For a nonstationary eigenoperator satisfying ℱdrv(Aj)=λjAj\mathcal F_{\mathrm{drv}}(A_j)=\lambda_jA_j, the exponential envelope rate at cycle endpoints is

Γjdrv=−log⁡|λj|τdrv,0<|λj|<1.\Gamma_j^{\mathrm{drv}} =-\frac{\log|\lambda_j|}{\tau_{\mathrm{drv}}}, \qquad 0<|\lambda_j|<1.(3.39)

Nontrivial Jordan blocks add polynomial factors, and the observed signal depends on the overlaps of the initial state and observable with each mode. Maintenance changes both the total elapsed duration and the cycle spectrum that determines relaxation. Thermalization of spatial motion additionally requires momentum exchange through contact.

These time scales assume a fixed environment temperature. When that temperature changes, the target thermal state moves as well. Whether the system follows it depends on the comparison between target motion and actual relaxation. This comparison connects fixed-temperature thermalization to cooling.

4. Cooling and Temperature Evolution

As matter releases energy to the environment, its energy distribution changes and the corresponding energy-based temperature falls. The relaxation times obtained in Chapter 3 determine whether the distribution can adjust sufficiently quickly. If the target thermal state specified by the environment preparation moves slowly enough, the system can remain close to a sequence of changing thermal states. If the target moves too fast, the actual distribution lags behind it. Cooling therefore involves both energy balance and internal relaxation.

This chapter uses the thermal cycle of Chapter 2 with the fixed energy operator HKH_K. Denote the inverse temperature of the environment preparation by βB\beta_{\mathrm B}, and the inverse temperature obtained by inverting the system’s mean-energy relation by βE\beta_E. The former enters the exchange and restoration preparations; the latter is read from the system state.

4.1 Temperature and Energy Distribution

On the full state space, the equilibrium energy at inverse temperature β\beta is

ZK(β)=∑j=0Kdje−βEj,dj=|Sj|,UK(β)=Tr⁡(HKρβ)=−∂βlog⁡ZK(β).\begin{aligned} Z_K(\beta)&=\sum_{j=0}^{K}d_j e^{-\beta E_j}, \qquad d_j=|S_j|,\\ U_K(\beta)&=\operatorname{Tr}(H_K\rho_\beta) =-\partial_\beta\log Z_K(\beta). \end{aligned}(4.1)

All independent states at each energy are included. Differentiating UKU_K once more gives

dUKdβ=−VK(β),VK(β)=Tr⁡(HK2ρβ)−UK(β)2.\begin{aligned} \frac{dU_K}{d\beta}&=-V_K(\beta),\\ V_K(\beta)&=\operatorname{Tr}(H_K^2\rho_\beta)-U_K(\beta)^2. \end{aligned}(4.2)

As long as distinct energies participate at finite temperature, VK>0V_K>0, and the equilibrium energy decreases strictly with β\beta. In terms of T=1/βT=1/\beta, the heat capacity is

CK(T)=dUKdT=β2VK(β)>0.C_K(T)=\frac{dU_K}{dT} =\beta^2V_K(\beta)>0.(4.3)

The actual state ρn\rho_n has mean energy En=Tr⁡(HKρn)E_n=\operatorname{Tr}(H_K\rho_n). On the positive-temperature branch 0<En<UK(0)0<E_n<U_K(0), the equations

UK(βE(n))=En,TE(n)=1βE(n)U_K(\beta_E(n))=E_n, \qquad T_E(n)=\frac{1}{\beta_E(n)}(4.4)

define a unique energy-based temperature. This provides a common reading for cooling curves. Whether the full distribution is close to the corresponding Gibbs state is still determined by ρn−ρβE(n)\rho_n-\rho_{\beta_E(n)}. The redistribution among equal-energy modes in Chapter 3 already shows that the same mean energy can correspond to different internal occupations.

The finite spectrum restricts the energy to 0≤En≤Klog⁡p0\le E_n\le K\log p. The partition function gives UK(0)=Tr⁡HK/dim⁡ℋKU_K(0)=\operatorname{Tr}H_K/\dim\mathcal H_K and UK(β)→0U_K(\beta)\to0 as β→+∞\beta\to+\infty. All temperature changes below are calculated along this finite-space energy curve.

4.2 Thermalization at Changing Temperature

Under the environment refreshing conditions of Section 1.2, let the incoming thermal environment in cycle nn have inverse temperature βB,n\beta_{\mathrm B,n}, and take the restoration shares at the same temperature, gn=π(βB,n)g_n=\pi(\beta_{\mathrm B,n}). Fix the other channel data and the total elapsed duration. Denote the actual cycle and its equilibrium state by

ℱn=ℱβB,n,ρn*=ρβB,n,ρn+1=ℱn(ρn),ℱn(ρn*)=ρn*.\begin{gathered} \mathcal F_n=\mathcal F_{\beta_{\mathrm B,n}},\qquad \rho_n^*=\rho_{\beta_{\mathrm B,n}},\\ \rho_{n+1}=\mathcal F_n(\rho_n),\qquad \mathcal F_n(\rho_n^*)=\rho_n^*. \end{gathered}(4.5)

Each cycle preserves its own target thermal state, but the next target can differ. Tracking instantaneous stationary states under slowly varying parameters is also studied in the adiabatic theory of contracting evolutions [15]. Setting δn=ρn−ρn*\delta_n=\rho_n-\rho_n^* and subtracting directly gives

δn+1=ℱn(δn)+ρn*−ρn+1*.\delta_{n+1} =\mathcal F_n(\delta_n)+\rho_n^*-\rho_{n+1}^*.(4.6)

The first term is the decay of the existing deviation during the current cycle; the second is the new deviation caused by target motion. Together they determine the actual lag.

Using the contraction decomposition of Chapter 2, let cn>0c_n>0 be the common-restoration lower bound for this cycle. With en=∥δn∥1e_n=\|\delta_n\|_1 and dn=∥ρn+1*−ρn*∥1d_n=\|\rho_{n+1}^*-\rho_n^*\|_1, we obtain

en+1≤(1−cn)en+dn,en≤e0∏k=0n−1(1−ck)+∑m=0n−1dm∏k=m+1n−1(1−ck).\begin{aligned} e_{n+1}&\le(1-c_n)e_n+d_n,\\ e_n&\le e_0\prod_{k=0}^{n-1}(1-c_k)\\ &\quad+\sum_{m=0}^{n-1}d_m \prod_{k=m+1}^{n-1}(1-c_k). \end{aligned}(4.7)

An empty product equals one. Each deviation produced by target motion is attenuated by the subsequent cycles.

Since HKH_K is fixed, the Gibbs-state derivative can be calculated separately at each energy:

∂βρβ=−(HK−UK(β))ρβ,∥∂βρβ∥1=Tr⁡(|HK−UK(β)|ρβ)≤VK(β).\begin{aligned} \partial_\beta\rho_\beta &=-(H_K-U_K(\beta))\rho_\beta,\\ \|\partial_\beta\rho_\beta\|_1 &=\operatorname{Tr}(|H_K-U_K(\beta)|\rho_\beta)\\ &\le\sqrt{V_K(\beta)}. \end{aligned}(4.8)

Thus, if InI_n is the interval between the inverse temperatures of adjacent cycles, the target displacement satisfies

dn≤|βB,n+1−βB,n|supβ∈InVK(β).d_n\le |\beta_{\mathrm B,n+1}-\beta_{\mathrm B,n}| \sup_{\beta\in I_n}\sqrt{V_K(\beta)}.(4.9)

On a fixed finite-temperature interval, if the actual channels maintain cn≥cmin>0c_n\ge c_{\min}>0 and dn≤dmaxd_n\le d_{\max}, the exact accumulated bound reduces to

en≤(1−cmin)ne0+dmaxcmin[1−(1−cmin)n].\begin{aligned} e_n&\le(1-c_{\min})^n e_0\\ &\quad+\frac{d_{\max}}{c_{\min}} \bigl[1-(1-c_{\min})^n\bigr]. \end{aligned}(4.10)

Once the initial-state contribution has decayed, dmax/cmin≪1d_{\max}/c_{\min}\ll1 is sufficient for tracking. When the temperature varies smoothly with sufficiently small changes per cycle, the corresponding approximate criterion is that the following ratio remain uniformly small over the interval considered:

τtot|β̇B|VK(βB)cmin≪1.\frac{\tau_{\mathrm{tot}}|\dot\beta_{\mathrm B}| \sqrt{V_K(\beta_{\mathrm B})}}{c_{\min}}\ll1.(4.11)

This sufficient condition controls the full-state deviation. If exit channels weaken upon cooling, tracking should instead be checked using the cycle-dependent cnc_n and the accumulated bound.

4.3 Energy Flow and Cooling Rate

Changes in environment temperature affect the system through actual exchanges. At the beginning of cycle nn, denote the matter occupations by xν(n)x_\nu(n) and the background endpoint occupations by za(n)z_a(n). When temperature changes, the incoming background still comes from the preceding output and generally differs from the restoration shares prescribed for the current cycle. The net channel exit must therefore be written as

Jaν(n)=ϵaν(βB,n)xν(n)−fνa(βB,n)za(n).J_{a\nu}(n) =\epsilon_{a\nu}(\beta_{\mathrm B,n})x_\nu(n) -f_{\nu a}(\beta_{\mathrm B,n})z_a(n).(4.12)

After thermal exchange, the background occupations and their total share are

z̃a=za+∑νJaν,ỹ=∑az̃a.\widetilde z_a=z_a+\sum_\nu J_{a\nu}, \qquad \widetilde y=\sum_a\widetilde z_a.(4.13)

Restoration then redistributes them as ỹπa(βB,n)\widetilde y\pi_a(\beta_{\mathrm B,n}). The energy balance of Chapter 2 holds cycle by cycle:

QT(n)=∑a,ν(Ea−Eν)Jaν(n),QR(n)=ỹE¯πn−∑aEaz̃a,E¯πn=∑aπa(βB,n)Ea,En+1−En=QT(n)+QR(n).\begin{aligned} Q_T(n)&=\sum_{a,\nu}(E_a-E_\nu)J_{a\nu}(n),\\ Q_R(n)&=\widetilde y\,\overline E_{\pi_n} -\sum_aE_a\widetilde z_a,\\ \overline E_{\pi_n}&=\sum_a\pi_a(\beta_{\mathrm B,n})E_a,\\ E_{n+1}-E_n&=Q_T(n)+Q_R(n). \end{aligned}(4.14)

The mean outward energy flow must therefore be read from the complete balance:

Pout(n)=−QT(n)+QR(n)τtot.P_{\mathrm{out}}(n) =-\frac{Q_T(n)+Q_R(n)}{\tau_{\mathrm{tot}}}.(4.15)

A positive Pout>0P_{\mathrm{out}}>0 means that the system loses energy during this cycle, lowering its energy-based temperature. Thermal exchange and background restoration can each absorb or release energy; their sum determines the actual cooling rate. Resources needed to change the environment preparation belong to the preparation apparatus. The quantity calculated here is the energy gained or lost by the system when that preparation interacts with it.

Since En=UK(βE(n))E_n=U_K(\beta_E(n)), the temperature change between adjacent endpoints satisfies the exact relation

∫βE(n)βE(n+1)VK(b)db=τtotPout(n).\int_{\beta_E(n)}^{\beta_E(n+1)} V_K(b)\,db =\tau_{\mathrm{tot}}P_{\mathrm{out}}(n).(4.16)

Positive outward energy flow raises the upper integration limit: βE\beta_E increases and TET_E decreases. On time scales for which temperature changes sufficiently little per cycle, the endpoint differences further give

VK(βE)β̇E=Pout,CK(TE)ṪE=−Pout.\begin{aligned} V_K(\beta_E)\,\dot\beta_E&=P_{\mathrm{out}},\\ C_K(T_E)\,\dot T_E&=-P_{\mathrm{out}}. \end{aligned}(4.17)

These relations convert actual energy output into temperature change. Energy flow follows from joint exchange and restoration, while heat capacity follows from the full Gibbs partition function. If the distribution also satisfies the tracking condition of the preceding section, the energy reading can describe the temperature of a system close to a thermal state.

4.4 Low-Temperature Cooling

These energy relations also apply to cooling that does not maintain thermal equilibrium. Consider a cycle in which matter modes exit to the zero-energy background and release energy to the environment. Take K≥2K\ge2, allow each matter mode to exchange only with the zero-energy background endpoint e0e_0, and take both the thermal environment and restoration preparations to the zero-temperature limit. Channel weights and exchange angles remain fixed, with a0>0a_0>0. For a positive-energy matter mode, Eν>0E_\nu>0 and E0−Eν=−EνE_0-E_\nu=-E_\nu, so

tu→1,tv→0,ϵν=a0νsin⁡2α0ν>0,fν0=0.\begin{aligned} t_u&\longrightarrow1,\qquad t_v\longrightarrow0,\\ \epsilon_\nu&=a_{0\nu}\sin^2\alpha_{0\nu}>0, \qquad f_{\nu0}=0. \end{aligned}(4.18)

At zero temperature, positive-energy modes can still exit by releasing energy, while reverse formation stops because the environment supplies no energy. The energy-absorbing exit channels of Section 3.5 are suppressed upon cooling. Zero-energy matter modes still exchange with e0e_0 at equal energy, with tu=tv=1/2t_u=t_v=1/2, without affecting total system energy. The restoration preparation tends to σsh=Pe0\sigma^{\mathrm{sh}}=P_{e_0}, transferring all positive background energy to the restoration auxiliary.

Take the state after the first completed cooling cycle as the time origin for this section. Thereafter, only matter modes carry positive energy. They receive no reverse-formation contribution, so the full occupation equations reduce directly to

xν(n)=(1−ϵν)nxν(0)(Eν>0),En=∑Eν>0Eνxν(0)(1−ϵν)n.\begin{aligned} x_\nu(n)&=(1-\epsilon_\nu)^n x_\nu(0) \quad(E_\nu>0),\\ E_n&=\sum_{E_\nu>0}E_\nu x_\nu(0) (1-\epsilon_\nu)^n. \end{aligned}(4.19)

If the excitation energy is initially nonzero at this time origin, it decreases through the output of each cycle and remains positive for any finite number of cycles. Let λE\lambda_E be the largest 1−ϵν1-\epsilon_\nu among initially occupied positive-energy modes, and let AE>0A_E>0 be the sum of all energy coefficients with that factor. The finite number of modes gives

En=AEe−ΓEtn[1+o(1)],ΓE=−log⁡λEτtot.\begin{gathered} E_n=A_Ee^{-\Gamma_E t_n}[1+o(1)],\\ \Gamma_E=-\frac{\log\lambda_E}{\tau_{\mathrm{tot}}}. \end{gathered}(4.20)

This energy decay rate depends on the actual exit channels and initial state. If all positive-energy modes have the same exit share ϵ\epsilon, then En=Einit(1−ϵ)nE_n=E_{\mathrm{init}}(1-\epsilon)^n holds from the time origin, without waiting for late-time dominance of a leading mode.

Converting this energy curve to a temperature reading requires the low-temperature form of the full spectrum. Let d0d_0 and d1d_1 be the degeneracies of the ground and first excited levels, respectively, and let Δ=log⁡p\Delta=\log p be the first excitation gap. For finite KK,

ZK(β)=d0+d1e−βΔ+O(e−2βΔ),UK(β)=Δd1d0e−βΔ[1+O(e−βΔ)].\begin{aligned} Z_K(\beta)&=d_0+d_1e^{-\beta\Delta} +O(e^{-2\beta\Delta}),\\ U_K(\beta)&=\Delta\frac{d_1}{d_0} e^{-\beta\Delta}[1+O(e^{-\beta\Delta})]. \end{aligned}(4.21)

Once the actual energy enters the positive-temperature branch, inversion of UK(βE(n))=EnU_K(\beta_E(n))=E_n gives the late-time relations

βE(n)=ΓEΔtn+1Δlog⁡Δd1d0AE+o(1).\begin{aligned} \beta_E(n) &=\frac{\Gamma_E}{\Delta}t_n +\frac{1}{\Delta}\log\frac{\Delta d_1}{d_0A_E} +o(1). \end{aligned}(4.22)
TE(n)∼ΔΓEtn.T_E(n)\sim\frac{\Delta}{\Gamma_E t_n}.(4.23)

Exponential energy decay corresponds to an inverse-time decrease of the temperature reading. The quantity ΓE\Gamma_E comes from the actual slow energy mode, while Δ\Delta is the first excitation gap of the full thermal distribution. The slowest energy mode need not lie at the lowest excited level; the two enter the result separately.

The inverse-time law follows from the zero-temperature exit rates and the finite spectrum. Changes in incoming temperature, reverse-formation channels, coupling, or duration require recalculation of the energy flow. Preparation times and resource constraints for the cold source are determined separately by the apparatus [16].

4.5 Corrections to the Cooling Curve

The approach to the inverse-time law also reflects the initial preparation and the other energy modes. Let u=e−βΔu=e^{-\beta\Delta}, r1=d1/d0r_1=d_1/d_0, and r2=d2/d0r_2=d_2/d_0. For fixed finite K≥2K\ge2, expanding the full partition function to second order gives

ZKd0=1+r1u+r2u2+O(u3),UKΔ=r1u+2r2u2+O(u3)1+r1u+r2u2+O(u3)=r1u+(2r2−r12)u2+O(u3).\begin{aligned} \frac{Z_K}{d_0}&=1+r_1u+r_2u^2+O(u^3),\\ \frac{U_K}{\Delta} &=\frac{r_1u+2r_2u^2+O(u^3)} {1+r_1u+r_2u^2+O(u^3)}\\ &=r_1u+(2r_2-r_1^2)u^2+O(u^3). \end{aligned}(4.24)

Writing x=E/Δx=E/\Delta and inverting order by order yields

u=xr1−2r2−r12r13x2+O(x3).u=\frac{x}{r_1} -\frac{2r_2-r_1^2}{r_1^3}x^2+O(x^3).(4.25)

Using ΔβE=−log⁡u\Delta\beta_E=-\log u, we then obtain

ΔβE=log⁡Δr1E+cGEΔ+O(E2Δ2),cG=2r2r12−1.\begin{aligned} \Delta\beta_E &=\log\frac{\Delta r_1}{E} +c_{\mathrm G}\frac{E}{\Delta} +O\!\left(\frac{E^2}{\Delta^2}\right),\\ c_{\mathrm G}&=\frac{2r_2}{r_1^2}-1. \end{aligned}(4.26)

This coefficient is determined by the full shell degeneracies. The first excited shell has r1=1/pr_1=1/p. For K=2K=2, the second excited shell is the terminal zero element, so r2=1/[p(p−1)]r_2=1/[p(p-1)] and cG=(p+1)/(p−1)c_{\mathrm G}=(p+1)/(p-1). For K>2K>2, the second excited shell is an ordinary shell, giving r2=1/p2r_2=1/p^2 and cG=1c_{\mathrm G}=1. The truncation boundary thus enters the first correction to temperature calibration.

Meanwhile, the positive-energy modes of the preceding section have rates Γν=−log⁡(1−ϵν)/τtot\Gamma_\nu=-\log(1-\epsilon_\nu)/\tau_{\mathrm{tot}}. Combining slow modes with the same rate into AEA_E, write the exact energy curve as

En=AEe−ΓEtn(1+ηn),ηn=∑Eν>0Γν>ΓEEνxν(0)AEe−(Γν−ΓE)tn≥0.\begin{aligned} E_n&=A_Ee^{-\Gamma_Et_n}(1+\eta_n),\\ \eta_n&=\sum_{\substack{E_\nu>0\\ \Gamma_\nu>\Gamma_E}} \frac{E_\nu x_\nu(0)}{A_E} e^{-(\Gamma_\nu-\Gamma_E)t_n}\ge0. \end{aligned}(4.27)

If no faster mode is occupied, ηn=0\eta_n=0. Substituting this curve into the temperature expansion and setting b0=log⁡(Δr1/AE)b_0=\log(\Delta r_1/A_E) gives

ΔβE(n)=ΓEtn+b0−log⁡(1+ηn)+cGEnΔ+O(En2Δ2).\begin{aligned} \Delta\beta_E(n) ={}&\Gamma_Et_n+b_0-\log(1+\eta_n)\\ &+c_{\mathrm G}\frac{E_n}{\Delta} +O\!\left(\frac{E_n^2}{\Delta^2}\right). \end{aligned}(4.28)

The effect of subleading slow modes on the energy curve appears in the temperature reading as −log⁡(1+ηn)-\log(1+\eta_n), while the finite partition function corrects the calibration through cGEn/Δc_{\mathrm G}E_n/\Delta. The leading decay rate of the former is the smallest positive rate difference Γν−ΓE\Gamma_\nu-\Gamma_E among occupied modes; the latter decays at rate ΓE\Gamma_E. Which contribution dominates depends on the actual spectrum, and coefficients must also be compared when the orders coincide. Retaining the full logarithm also includes higher-order terms of this spectral correction.

The constant b0b_0 retains the initial energy weight. Since TE=1/βET_E=1/\beta_E, even when only one energy decay rate remains, finite-time deviations from the inverse-time law can be examined using the shifted hyperbola:

ΔΓEtn+b0=ΔΓEtn−Δb0(ΓEtn)2+O(tn−3).\begin{aligned} \frac{\Delta}{\Gamma_Et_n+b_0} &=\frac{\Delta}{\Gamma_Et_n} -\frac{\Delta b_0}{(\Gamma_Et_n)^2} +O(t_n^{-3}). \end{aligned}(4.29)

The initial-condition intercept, actual energy spectrum, and temperature calibration separately affect the finite-time curve. Away from the low-temperature regime, the full partition function should be inverted directly.

As energy decreases, auxiliary outputs from each cycle retain the corresponding exchange information. Energy flow determines how the system cools; the outputs and their correlations further explain how the system continually loses its dependence on the initial state while the complete joint evolution remains reversible.

5. Irreversibility of Thermalization

Thermalization changes the energy and internal composition of the system and carries distinctions between processes into auxiliary outputs. Once old outputs depart, the system continues exchanging with independently prepared fresh environments and gradually loses its dependence on the initial state. Retaining all outputs and their correlations in the joint description leaves the evolution reversible. The direction of the system’s approach to thermal equilibrium follows from the entropy balance of the same complete cycle.

5.1 Exchange Records

Denote the system and full auxiliary space after one cycle by SS and ℰ\mathcal E. Their final joint state and system marginal are

Ωnout=𝕌tot(ρn⊗ηfull)𝕌tot†,ρn+1=Tr⁡ℰΩnout.\begin{aligned} \Omega_n^{\mathrm{out}} &=\mathbb U_{\mathrm{tot}} (\rho_n\otimes\eta_{\mathrm{full}}) \mathbb U_{\mathrm{tot}}^\dagger,\\ \rho_{n+1}&=\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathcal E}\Omega_n^{\mathrm{out}}. \end{aligned}(5.1)

Exchange, return, and background restoration are all included in this final state. Coherent retrieval first returns the same auxiliary to its initial preparation, transferring back to the system the directional distinctions it carried during the process. Background restoration subsequently preserves background distinctions in that auxiliary’s output labels. Records must therefore be assessed from the states left by the thermal environment and auxiliary at the end of the complete cycle [1].

Let ωα\omega_\alpha be the normalized conditional environment state for process component α\alpha, and let r=f(α)r=f(\alpha) be the recorded category. Let Πrrec\Pi_r^{\mathrm{rec}} be the orthogonal projections of the actual pointer, including the no-response outcome. A complete record of the selected categories satisfies

ΠrrecΠsrec=δrsΠrrec,∑rΠrrec=Iℰ.\Pi_r^{\mathrm{rec}}\Pi_s^{\mathrm{rec}} =\delta_{rs}\Pi_r^{\mathrm{rec}},\qquad \sum_r\Pi_r^{\mathrm{rec}}=I_{\mathcal E}.(5.2)
Πrrecωα=δr,f(α)ωα.\Pi_r^{\mathrm{rec}}\omega_\alpha =\delta_{r,f(\alpha)}\omega_\alpha.(5.3)

These distinctions must also have nonzero output shares and must not be mixed by subsequent actions during storage. Extend the record projections by the identity on the remaining spaces, writing Π̂rrec\widehat\Pi_r^{\mathrm{rec}}. The storage condition is

Upost†Π̂rrecUpost=Π̂rrec.U_{\mathrm{post}}^\dagger\widehat\Pi_r^{\mathrm{rec}} U_{\mathrm{post}}=\widehat\Pi_r^{\mathrm{rec}}.(5.4)

This holds when old outputs no longer participate in system exchange and storage operations preserve the pointer labels [17]. Records are formed by the actual joint action, and their existence does not depend on whether anyone reads them. If conditional states are only partially distinguishable, the accessible information resolves only part of the distinctions, and their actual overlaps must be retained.

Thermal exchange gives a concrete example. Retaining the channel and incoming energy-level labels and comparing the outgoing level identifies exit and reverse formation and reveals the environment energy change. Restoration-auxiliary labels distinguish background endpoints before and after restoration. Reading only the outgoing energy level without retaining the incoming label generally does not determine the energy change of that exchange. Record resolution is thus determined by the distinctions actually preserved and cannot be replaced by an arbitrary choice of operators or representation.
