The coherence decay of Chapter 3 is also determined by overlaps of these final states. If a pure joint component is written as ∑iAi|i⟩|ηi⟩\sum_i A_i|i\rangle|\eta_i\rangle, where |ηi⟩|\eta_i\rangle are conditional environment states, then

⟨i|ρ′|j⟩=AiAj¯⟨ηj|ηi⟩.\langle i|\rho'|j\rangle =A_i\overline{A_j}\langle\eta_j|\eta_i\rangle.(5.5)

Orthogonal outputs remove the corresponding cross terms from the system marginal; coincident outputs preserve coherence. Departed records and their correlations with the system and other outputs remain part of the joint state. Local information loss and preservation of joint information thus occur within the same process.

5.2 Entropy and Thermal Equilibrium

First fix a finite positive inverse temperature β\beta, take restoration shares g=πg=\pi, and hold all other cycle data fixed. The system approaches the full Gibbs state ρβ=e−βHK/ZK\rho_\beta=e^{-\beta H_K}/Z_K obtained in Chapter 2. We use von Neumann entropy and quantum relative entropy [18],

S(ρ)=−Tr⁡(ρlog⁡ρ),D(ρ‖σ)=Tr⁡[ρ(log⁡ρ−log⁡σ)].\begin{aligned} S(\rho)&=-\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\log\rho),\\ D(\rho\Vert\sigma) &=\operatorname{Tr}[\rho(\log\rho-\log\sigma)]. \end{aligned}(5.6)

We use the convention 0log⁡0=00\log0=0. At finite temperature, ρβ\rho_\beta has full rank, so every system state has finite relative entropy with respect to it. Substituting the logarithm of the Gibbs state yields

D(ρ‖ρβ)=−S(ρ)+βTr⁡(HKρ)+log⁡ZK.D(\rho\Vert\rho_\beta) =-S(\rho)+\beta\operatorname{Tr}(H_K\rho)+\log Z_K.(5.7)

This includes both energy and the degree of internal mixing. The system’s own entropy can decrease during cooling; the direction of approach to equilibrium is measured by deviation from the same thermal state.

The complete cycle is completely positive, trace-preserving, and preserves ρβ\rho_\beta. The data-processing inequality for relative entropy [19] therefore gives

D(ρn+1‖ρβ)=D(ℱπρn‖ℱπρβ)≤D(ρn‖ρβ).\begin{aligned} D(\rho_{n+1}\Vert\rho_\beta) &=D(\mathcal F_\pi\rho_n\Vert\mathcal F_\pi\rho_\beta)\\ &\le D(\rho_n\Vert\rho_\beta). \end{aligned}(5.8)

Let Dn=D(ρn‖ρβ)D_n=D(\rho_n\Vert\rho_\beta). Expanding this quantity as above and using the complete energy balance of Chapter 4, the relaxation entropy production per cycle is

Σn=Dn−Dn+1=S(ρn+1)−S(ρn)−β[QT(n)+QR(n)]≥0.\begin{aligned} \Sigma_n&=D_n-D_{n+1}\\ &=S(\rho_{n+1})-S(\rho_n)\\ &\quad-\beta[Q_T(n)+Q_R(n)]\ge0. \end{aligned}(5.9)

This relation includes energy flow in both thermal exchange and background restoration. Retaining only one contribution no longer gives the change of the full state relative to thermal equilibrium.

The common-restoration share of Chapter 2 also establishes strictness. Write σ=σπsh\sigma=\sigma_\pi^{\mathrm{sh}} and use ℱπ(A)=cTr⁡(A)σ+(1−c)𝒢π(A)\mathcal F_\pi(A)=c\operatorname{Tr}(A)\sigma+(1-c)\mathcal G_\pi(A), where c>0c>0 and 𝒢π\mathcal G_\pi is completely positive and trace-preserving. Joint convexity of relative entropy [19] first gives

D(ℱπρ‖ρβ)=D(cσ+(1−c)𝒢πρ‖cσ+(1−c)𝒢πρβ)≤(1−c)D(𝒢πρ‖𝒢πρβ)≤(1−c)D(ρ‖ρβ).\begin{aligned} D(\mathcal F_\pi\rho\Vert\rho_\beta) &=D\bigl(c\sigma+(1-c)\mathcal G_\pi\rho\\ &\qquad\Vert c\sigma+(1-c)\mathcal G_\pi\rho_\beta\bigr)\\ &\le(1-c)D(\mathcal G_\pi\rho\Vert\mathcal G_\pi\rho_\beta)\\ &\le(1-c)D(\rho\Vert\rho_\beta). \end{aligned}(5.10)

The last step again uses data processing. Hence,

Dn≤(1−c)nD0,Σn≥cDn≥0.\begin{gathered} D_n\le(1-c)^nD_0,\\ \Sigma_n\ge cD_n\ge0. \end{gathered}(5.11)

Relative entropy decreases strictly whenever the system is not yet at thermal equilibrium. This statement applies to the full density operator, including occupations and coherences. The constant cc gives a uniform estimate; actual decay rates remain determined by the modes in Chapter 3.

Summing over cycles cancels intermediate terms:

∑n=0N−1Σn=D0−DN→D0.\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\Sigma_n=D_0-D_N \longrightarrow D_0.(5.12)

For a fixed environment, a finite initial deviation contributes only a finite accumulated relaxation entropy production. Denoting nonequilibrium free energy at this temperature by ℱβ(ρ)=Tr⁡(HKρ)−β−1S(ρ)\mathscr F_\beta(\rho)=\operatorname{Tr}(H_K\rho)-\beta^{-1}S(\rho), the same result is

D(ρ‖ρβ)=β[ℱβ(ρ)−ℱβ(ρβ)],ℱβ(ρn)−ℱβ(ρn+1)=β−1Σn.\begin{gathered} D(\rho\Vert\rho_\beta) =\beta[\mathscr F_\beta(\rho)-\mathscr F_\beta(\rho_\beta)],\\ \mathscr F_\beta(\rho_n)-\mathscr F_\beta(\rho_{n+1}) =\beta^{-1}\Sigma_n. \end{gathered}(5.13)

When the environment temperature changes, the target thermal state moves as well. A nonnegative Σn\Sigma_n can still be defined relative to the target ρβn\rho_{\beta_n} of each cycle, where βn=βB,n\beta_n=\beta_{\mathrm B,n}. Expanding the Gibbs-state logarithms for a moving target gives

D(ρn+1‖ρβn+1)−D(ρn‖ρβn)=−Σn+(βn+1−βn)En+1+log⁡ZK(βn+1)−log⁡ZK(βn).\begin{aligned} &D(\rho_{n+1}\Vert\rho_{\beta_{n+1}}) -D(\rho_n\Vert\rho_{\beta_n})\\ &\quad=-\Sigma_n+(\beta_{n+1}-\beta_n)E_{n+1}\\ &\qquad+\log Z_K(\beta_{n+1})-\log Z_K(\beta_n). \end{aligned}(5.14)

Thermalization reduces the deviation from the current equilibrium state in each cycle, while cooling changes the next target. Together they determine the actual lag. This relation applies at finite temperature. The zero-temperature reference state is not full rank, so the zero-temperature cooling curves of Chapter 4 continue to be calculated from the actual energy equations.

5.3 Entropy Balance of the Environment

At system equilibrium, relaxation entropy production vanishes, while auxiliary preparations may still change. Treating all auxiliaries of one cycle as a whole, the independent input is Ωin=ρ⊗ηℰ\Omega_{\mathrm{in}}=\rho\otimes\eta_{\mathcal E}. Joint unitary evolution preserves its spectrum, so S(Ωout)=S(ρ)+S(ηℰ)S(\Omega_{\mathrm{out}})=S(\rho)+S(\eta_{\mathcal E}). The definition of mutual information gives

ΔSS+ΔSℰ=I(S:ℰ)out,I(S:ℰ)out=S(ρ′)+S(ηℰ′)−S(Ωout).\begin{aligned} \Delta S_S+\Delta S_{\mathcal E} &=I(S:\mathcal E)_{\mathrm{out}},\\ I(S:\mathcal E)_{\mathrm{out}} &=S(\rho')+S(\eta_{\mathcal E}')-S(\Omega_{\mathrm{out}}). \end{aligned}(5.15)

Joint entropy is unchanged, while the increase in the sum of the marginal entropies equals the correlations created. Information can reside in an individual output or in correlations between the system and outputs or among different outputs. Nonzero mutual information signifies correlation; whether it constitutes a storable record is still determined by the criteria of Section 5.1.

The two environment preparations in the complete cycle differ, and so do the sources of their entropy balances. The thermal environment has a Gibbs preparation at the same temperature within each direct-sum block, and thermal exchange preserves the block weights. The blockwise normalization constants in log⁡ηT\log\eta_T therefore cancel between the final and initial states. Since the environment energy change is −QT-Q_T, we obtain [1,20,21]

D(ηT′‖ηT)=−ΔST−βQT,ΔSthsys−βQT=IT+D(ηT′‖ηT)≥0.\begin{aligned} D(\eta_T'\Vert\eta_T)&=-\Delta S_T-\beta Q_T,\\ \Delta S_{\mathrm{th}}^{\mathrm{sys}}-\beta Q_T &=I_T+D(\eta_T'\Vert\eta_T)\ge0. \end{aligned}(5.16)

Here ITI_T is the mutual information between the system and thermal environment at the end of thermal exchange. The two terms on the right account for correlations created during exchange and changes in the thermal environment relative to its initial preparation.

First use the pure restoration preparation of Section 2.5. The complete restoration environment is R=AQDR=AQD, with input Pg=|g⟩⟨g|P_g=|g\rangle\langle g| and energy HR=HA+HQH_R=H_A+H_Q, including the zero-energy pointer. Since QQ is a spectator during restoration, ΔER=ΔEA=−QR\Delta E_R=\Delta E_A=-Q_R.

Denote the background block after thermal exchange by yξ𝒞y\xi_{\mathcal C}, where yy is the total background share and ξ𝒞\xi_{\mathcal C} is normalized. In the interaction picture of restoration, |eb,g⟩↦∑aπa|ea,rab⟩|e_b,g\rangle\mapsto\sum_a\sqrt{\pi_a}|e_a,r_{ab}\rangle transfers the input matrix structure into distinct auxiliary blocks. Its final state and entropy are therefore

ηR′=(1−y)Pg⊕⨁ayπaξ𝒞,S(ηR′)=h2(y)+y[𝖧(π)+S(ξ𝒞)].\begin{aligned} \eta_R'&=(1-y)P_g\ \oplus\ \bigoplus_a y\pi_a\xi_{\mathcal C},\\ S(\eta_R')&=h_2(y)+y[\mathsf H(\pi)+S(\xi_{\mathcal C})]. \end{aligned}(5.17)

Here h2(y)=−ylog⁡y−(1−y)log⁡(1−y)h_2(y)=-y\log y-(1-y)\log(1-y) and 𝖧(π)=−∑aπalog⁡πa\mathsf H(\pi)=-\sum_a\pi_a\log\pi_a. For y=0y=0, zero-weight terms are understood by continuity. The complete free evolution further conjugates the final auxiliary state by e−iτtotHRe^{-i\tau_{\mathrm{tot}}H_R}, leaving its spectrum, entropy, and energy unchanged. Restoration establishes the prescribed background distribution in the system while retaining the original background distinctions in the auxiliary.

To quantify the preparation change, take the full-rank comparison state ωR=e−βHR/ZR\omega_R=e^{-\beta H_R}/Z_R at the same finite temperature and define

CR=D(Pg‖ωR)−D(ηR′‖ωR).C_R=D(P_g\Vert\omega_R)-D(\eta_R'\Vert\omega_R).(5.18)

Expanding the two relative entropies for the pure input PgP_g and using the restoration-auxiliary energy change −QR-Q_R gives

CR=S(ηR′)+βQR.C_R=S(\eta_R')+\beta Q_R.(5.19)

The independent pure auxiliary input in the restoration stage also gives ΔSRsys=IR−S(ηR′)\Delta S_R^{\mathrm{sys}}=I_R-S(\eta_R'). Adding thermal exchange and restoration, with the system’s unitary phase from the coherent round trip leaving its entropy unchanged, yields the complete balance

Σn+CR=IT+D(ηT′‖ηT)+IR≥0.\Sigma_n+C_R =I_T+D(\eta_T'\Vert\eta_T)+I_R\ge0.(5.20)

The quantities ITI_T and IRI_R belong to the two separate stages. Their sum also includes final correlations between the thermal environment and restoration auxiliary, so it cannot simply be replaced by the final mutual information between the system and the entire environment. The term CRC_R describes the change in auxiliary preparation relative to the same comparison state; its sign is determined by the actual states and energy flows. Repreparing auxiliaries involves information reset and its physical cost [22], while the actual work required depends on the preparation operation.

When the system is already in ρβ\rho_\beta, thermal exchange preserves the joint input, giving IT=D(ηT′‖ηT)=QT=0I_T=D(\eta_T'\Vert\eta_T)=Q_T=0. Restoration preserves the system thermal state, with QR=Σn=0Q_R=\Sigma_n=0. Nevertheless, the restoration auxiliary changes from a pure state into an output carrying correlations. Setting y*=Z𝒞/ZKy_*=Z_{\mathcal C}/Z_K and ξ𝒞=σπsh\xi_{\mathcal C}=\sigma_\pi^{\mathrm{sh}}, the preceding relation gives

CR=IR=h2(y*)+2y*𝖧(π)>0.C_R=I_R=h_2(y_*)+2y_*\mathsf H(\pi)>0.(5.21)

If the apparatus prepares a mixed thermal reference ηA\eta_A and a blank pointer without supplying QQ, the system channel is unchanged, but the environment balance must be recalculated from the mixed input. At equilibrium input, the reference has marginal ηA\eta_A both before and after restoration, and the pointer distinguishes only the directional and background branches. Hence,

I(S:AD)mixed=h2(y*),I(S:AQD)pure=h2(y*)+2y*𝖧(π).\begin{aligned} I(S:AD)_{\mathrm{mixed}}&=h_2(y_*),\\ I(S:AQD)_{\mathrm{pure}}&=h_2(y_*)+2y_*\mathsf H(\pi). \end{aligned}(5.22)

With the pure preparation, the background branch correlates the system with purification register QQ, contributing 2y*𝖧(π)2y_*\mathsf H(\pi) after weighting by that branch. The same system restoration channel can therefore have different environment entropy balances, determined by the preparation and joint output.

If label-copying or storage devices are also used, their degrees of freedom enter the environment and the same joint entropy relation applies.

5.4 Forward and Reverse Processes and the Direction of Time

The direction of mean entropy production can also be expressed through recordable exchange trajectories. Forward-to-reverse probability ratios are central quantities in heat-exchange fluctuation relations [23]. Take an initial state diagonal in the common mode basis {ν,ea}\{\nu,e_a\}, with strictly positive initial shares in every mode, and retain the initial mode, incoming and outgoing thermal-exchange labels, and restoration labels. The conditional operators are diagonal operators or individual matrix units, so each recorded history tracks mode continuation and transfer. We group records by mode path and sum unresolved auxiliary labels within each path. Summing over all paths then recovers the established diagonal occupation dynamics.

Let 𝖡ji\mathsf B_{ji} be the thermal-exchange share from mode ii to jj, and 𝖱kj\mathsf R_{kj} the subsequent restoration share from jj to kk. Their nonzero entries are

𝖡ea,ν=ϵaν,𝖡ν,ea=fνa,𝖡ν,ν=1−ϵν,𝖡ea,ea=1−∑νfνa,𝖱eb,ea=πb,𝖱ν,ν=1.\begin{aligned} \mathsf B_{e_a,\nu}&=\epsilon_{a\nu},& \mathsf B_{\nu,e_a}&=f_{\nu a},\\ \mathsf B_{\nu,\nu}&=1-\epsilon_\nu,& \mathsf B_{e_a,e_a}&=1-\sum_\nu f_{\nu a},\\ \mathsf R_{e_b,e_a}&=\pi_b,& \mathsf R_{\nu,\nu}&=1. \end{aligned}(5.23)

Every column sums to one, and other entries vanish. Let qi=e−βEi/ZKq_i=e^{-\beta E_i}/Z_K be the full Gibbs shares. The forward-to-reverse exchange ratio and same-temperature restoration shares give, respectively,

𝖡jiqi=𝖡ijqj,𝖱kjqj=𝖱jkqk.\mathsf B_{ji}q_i=\mathsf B_{ij}q_j, \qquad \mathsf R_{kj}q_j=\mathsf R_{jk}q_k.(5.24)

A forward cycle performs exchange before restoration, with occupation kernel 𝖯F=𝖱𝖡\mathsf P_{\mathrm F}=\mathsf R\mathsf B. To compare trajectories in the opposite order, take the process 𝖯R=𝖡𝖱\mathsf P_{\mathrm R}=\mathsf B\mathsf R, which restores before exchanging. Each stage separately satisfies detailed balance; their product need not satisfy detailed balance in the same stage order.

For a one-cycle path i→j→ki\to j\to k with nonzero share, the paired reverse-order path is k→j→ik\to j\to i. Multiplying the two stage ratios cancels the intermediate mode weight:

𝖡ji𝖱kj𝖱jk𝖡ij=qkqi=eβ(Ei−Ek).\frac{\mathsf B_{ji}\mathsf R_{kj}} {\mathsf R_{jk}\mathsf B_{ij}} =\frac{q_k}{q_i} =e^{\beta(E_i-E_k)}.(5.25)

The quantity Ei−EkE_i-E_k is the combined energy released to the auxiliaries through thermal exchange and restoration.

Let ω\omega contain the mode sequence and intermediate endpoints over NN cycles. The forward process starts from p0p_0 and ends in pNp_N. The reverse-order comparison starts from pNp_N, traverses the stages in the opposite order, and follows the paired path ω‾\bar\omega. Endpoint shares and conditional transition shares give

ℙF[ω]=p0(i0)∏n=0N−1𝖡jnin𝖱in+1jn,ℙR[ω‾]=pN(iN)∏n=0N−1𝖱jnin+1𝖡injn.\begin{aligned} \mathbb P_{\mathrm F}[\omega] &=p_0(i_0)\prod_{n=0}^{N-1} \mathsf B_{j_n i_n}\mathsf R_{i_{n+1}j_n},\\ \mathbb P_{\mathrm R}[\bar\omega] &=p_N(i_N)\prod_{n=0}^{N-1} \mathsf R_{j_n i_{n+1}}\mathsf B_{i_nj_n}. \end{aligned}(5.26)

The logarithmic path-probability ratio is then

σ[ω]=log⁡ℙF[ω]ℙR[ω‾]=log⁡p0(i0)pN(iN)+β(Ei0−EiN).\begin{aligned} \sigma[\omega] &=\log\frac{\mathbb P_{\mathrm F}[\omega]} {\mathbb P_{\mathrm R}[\bar\omega]}\\ &=\log\frac{p_0(i_0)}{p_N(i_N)} +\beta(E_{i_0}-E_{i_N}). \end{aligned}(5.27)

The forward and reverse shares have matching support. Grouping paired paths by σ\sigma yields the detailed and integral fluctuation relations [24,25]

𝒫F(s)𝒫R(−s)=es,⟨e−σ⟩F=1.\begin{gathered} \frac{\mathcal P_{\mathrm F}(s)}{\mathcal P_{\mathrm R}(-s)}=e^s,\\ \left\langle e^{-\sigma}\right\rangle_{\mathrm F}=1. \end{gathered}(5.28)

The reverse-process variable is defined with the opposite sign on paired paths, and its endpoint comparison still uses pN,p0p_N,p_0 above. The denominator is the distribution for the specified reverse-order process; it cannot in general be replaced by the distribution of negative values in the same forward process. Under the forward path average, the initial and final modes are distributed according to p0,pNp_0,p_N, so

⟨σ⟩F=S(pN)−S(p0)+β[ES(0)−ES(N)]=D(p0‖q)−D(pN‖q)=∑n=0N−1Σn≥0.\begin{aligned} \langle\sigma\rangle_{\mathrm F} &=S(p_N)-S(p_0)+\beta[E_S(0)-E_S(N)]\\ &=D(p_0\Vert q)-D(p_N\Vert q)\\ &=\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\Sigma_n\ge0. \end{aligned}(5.29)

A single trajectory can have negative σ\sigma, while the mean direction remains consistent with relaxation of the full state. This relation concerns system relaxation along diagonal trajectories; changes in auxiliary preparations are still accounted for by Section 5.3. For general coherent initial states, the quantum-relative-entropy result of Section 5.2 applies directly.

Under the environment refreshing conditions of Section 1.2, all cycles can still be included in one joint unitary evolution. Retain every output and its coherent correlations over NN cycles, including the actual recording units. Denote the initial joint state by Ω(0)\Omega^{(0)} and the joint evolution by 𝕍N=𝕌N⋯𝕌1\mathbb V_N=\mathbb U_N\cdots\mathbb U_1. Then

𝕍N†Ω(N)𝕍N=Ω(0).\mathbb V_N^\dagger\Omega^{(N)}\mathbb V_N=\Omega^{(0)}.(5.30)

Realizing this recovery requires the actual final joint state and inverse actions in the opposite order. Continuing to supply independent fresh auxiliaries does not implement that inverse process. Chapter 2 shows that the trace distance between any two distinct system initial states contracts by a factor no greater than 1−c1-c. Trace-norm contraction of subsequent system channels [26] prevents universal recovery of that distance, so no physical system-only inverse channel works for every initial state. The local time direction of thermalization is jointly determined by the complete dynamics and environment refreshing conditions. Preserved records allow earlier distinctions to remain readable.

6. Tests of the Thermalization Mechanism

Testing the thermalization mechanism requires connecting a single energy exchange to the relaxation that follows. Once the exchange shares, environment preparations, and interaction durations are fixed, the same complete cycle jointly constrains the equilibrium distribution, occupation relaxation, coherence decay, and energy output. Reading these quantities separately tests whether they can be explained by one set of dynamical parameters. Changing whether old environments return further tests the environmental conditions on which repeated thermalization depends.

6.1 Exchange Statistics

Separately prepare matter mode ν\nu and background endpoint eae_a, and repeat one complete cycle with the same environment preparation and exchange action. Following the record criteria of Chapter 5, retain incoming and outgoing thermal-environment labels and count exit and reverse-formation events in the thermal-exchange stage. Let Nν,NeaN_\nu,N_{e_a} be the total trial counts for the two initial preparations. The corresponding event counts give

ϵ̂aν=Nν→eaNν,f̂νa=Nea→νNea.\widehat\epsilon_{a\nu} =\frac{N_{\nu\to e_a}}{N_\nu},\qquad \widehat f_{\nu a} =\frac{N_{e_a\to\nu}}{N_{e_a}}.(6.1)

The denominators include all trials, including no-response outcomes and transitions into other channels. These are thermal-exchange events and cannot be identified by substituting system background labels measured after restoration. Normalizing only within the selected channel’s sample would omit its preparation weight from the measured share.

For independent repeated preparations and sufficiently large samples, the counting shares approach the actual exchange shares of Chapter 2. Independently calibrated channel weights, incoming energy-level distributions, and exchange angles predict

ϵaν=aaνtu(aν)sin⁡2αaν,fνa=aaνtv(aν)sin⁡2αaν.\begin{aligned} \epsilon_{a\nu}&=a_{a\nu}t_u^{(a\nu)}\sin^2\alpha_{a\nu},\\ f_{\nu a}&=a_{a\nu}t_v^{(a\nu)}\sin^2\alpha_{a\nu}. \end{aligned}(6.2)

Their ratio cancels the common interaction strength, leaving the relation between energy difference and environment temperature:

log⁡ϵaνfνa=−β(Ea−Eν).\log\frac{\epsilon_{a\nu}}{f_{\nu a}} =-\beta(E_a-E_\nu).(6.3)

Repeating the measurement for different energy differences should give the same β\beta under a common-temperature preparation. Zero-energy-difference channels test equality of the two shares but cannot alone determine temperature. Raw forward and reverse event counts during equilibrium also include the respective initial occupations. Their equality indicates zero net flow; their ratio cannot be identified directly with the conditional-share ratio above.

Restoration-auxiliary labels can independently determine the background distribution. Conditional on trials that actually enter restoration, count the output endpoints to obtain ĝa\widehat g_a. The restoration distribution required at the common temperature is

πa=e−βEaZ𝒞,Z𝒞=∑be−βEb.\pi_a=\frac{e^{-\beta E_a}}{Z_{\mathcal C}},\qquad Z_{\mathcal C}=\sum_b e^{-\beta E_b}.(6.4)

Comparing ĝ\widehat g with π\pi at the temperature determined by the exchange ratios directly tests the same-temperature restoration condition of Section 2.3.

6.2 Joint Tests of Occupations and Coherence

Substituting the measured shares into the occupation matrix of Chapter 3, with time counted from the restored endpoint used there, predicts occupations over many cycles. The required parameters are

ϵν=∑aϵaν,bν=∑agafνa,fΣ=∑νbν,xν*y*=bνϵν.\begin{aligned} \epsilon_\nu&=\sum_a\epsilon_{a\nu},& b_\nu&=\sum_a g_af_{\nu a},\\ f_\Sigma&=\sum_\nu b_\nu,& \frac{x_\nu^*}{y_*}&=\frac{b_\nu}{\epsilon_\nu}. \end{aligned}(6.5)

The same matrix gives equilibrium shares and the decay factors of all occupation deviations. When N≥2N\ge2 and all matter modes have the same exit share ϵν=ϵ\epsilon_\nu=\epsilon, the total-share deviation and internal-composition deviations satisfy

yn−y*=λtotn(y0−y*),zν,n=λcompnzν,0,λtot=1−ϵ−fΣ,λcomp=1−ϵ.\begin{aligned} y_n-y_*&=\lambda_{\mathrm{tot}}^n(y_0-y_*),\\ z_{\nu,n}&=\lambda_{\mathrm{comp}}^n z_{\nu,0},\\ \lambda_{\mathrm{tot}}&=1-\epsilon-f_\Sigma,\qquad \lambda_{\mathrm{comp}}=1-\epsilon. \end{aligned}(6.6)

Here zν=xν−(bν/fΣ)(1−y)z_\nu=x_\nu-(b_\nu/f_\Sigma)(1-y). Different initial preparations can excite the two kinds of deviations separately. Changes in composition among equal-energy modes do not appear in mean energy, so the corresponding mode occupations must still be read.

Coherence supplies another independent reading. Under the same conditions, prepare a superposition of ν,μ\nu,\mu, evolve for nn cycles, and measure at the final endpoint in the states

|±θ⟩=|ν⟩±e−iθ|μ⟩2.|\pm_\theta\rangle =\frac{|\nu\rangle\pm e^{-i\theta}|\mu\rangle}{\sqrt2}.(6.7)

Treat results outside this subspace as a third outcome and normalize by the total number of trials. The probability difference between the two projections is

Cθ(n)=P+(n)−P−(n)=2Re⁡[e−iθρνμ(n)],C0(n)+iCπ/2(n)=2ρνμ(n).\begin{aligned} C_\theta(n)&=P_+(n)-P_-(n)\\ &=2\operatorname{Re}[e^{-i\theta}\rho_{\nu\mu}(n)],\\ C_0(n)+iC_{\pi/2}(n)&=2\rho_{\nu\mu}(n). \end{aligned}(6.8)

Measurements at the two phase settings therefore determine the real and imaginary parts of this matrix element. Retaining only samples that remain in the two-mode subspace would additionally divide the reading by xν+xμx_\nu+x_\mu, changing the decay law under test.

For the complete cycle of Chapter 3 and initial state |+0⟩|+_0\rangle,

Cθ(n)=γνμncos⁡[n(φν−φμ)−θ],γνμ=1−∑aϵaν1+cos⁡αaν−∑aϵaμ1+cos⁡αaμ.\begin{aligned} C_\theta(n)&=\gamma_{\nu\mu}^{\,n} \cos[n(\varphi_\nu-\varphi_\mu)-\theta],\\ \gamma_{\nu\mu} &=1-\sum_a\frac{\epsilon_{a\nu}}{1+\cos\alpha_{a\nu}}\\ &\quad-\sum_a\frac{\epsilon_{a\mu}}{1+\cos\alpha_{a\mu}}. \end{aligned}(6.9)

The phase difference comes jointly from free evolution and coherent retrieval over the complete cycle, while the coherence envelope and exit shares are constrained by the same exchange angles. Knowing only a total exit share is insufficient. Once channel-resolved shares and exchange angles are independently determined, the coherence curve provides an additional test.

Figure 6-1 uses the seven-dimensional example of Chapter 3: five zero-energy matter modes exchange only with the zero-energy background endpoint, each with weight 2/152/15. The preparation weight for no thermal exchange is 1/31/3, and restoration shares are (4/5,1/5)(4/5,1/5). Varying the common angle 0<α<π/20<\alpha<\pi/2 gives ϵ=sin⁡2α/15\epsilon=\sin^2\alpha/15 and fΣ=4ϵf_\Sigma=4\epsilon. Eliminating α\alpha requires the three per-cycle factors to lie on the same set of curves:

λtot=1−5ϵ,λcomp=1−ϵ,γνμ=1−215(1−1−15ϵ).\begin{aligned} \lambda_{\mathrm{tot}}&=1-5\epsilon,\\ \lambda_{\mathrm{comp}}&=1-\epsilon,\\ \gamma_{\nu\mu} &=1-\frac{2}{15}\bigl(1-\sqrt{1-15\epsilon}\bigr). \end{aligned}(6.10)

Conversion to physical time uses Γ=−log⁡λ/τtot\Gamma=-\log\lambda/\tau_{\mathrm{tot}}, taking λ=γνμ\lambda=\gamma_{\nu\mu} for the coherence envelope. The total elapsed duration must be measured independently. If changing the exchange angle also changes the cycle period, a change in the per-cycle factor cannot be identified directly with a change in the decay rate per unit time.

6.3 Cooling and Entropy Balance

Energy tests connect system changes to actual environment outputs. Incoming and outgoing thermal-environment energies and the initial and final restoration-auxiliary energies separately determine the energy transferred to the system in the two stages. If the mean system energy is EnE_n, one can independently compare

QT(n)=−Δ⟨HT⟩n,QR(n)=−Δ⟨HR⟩n,En+1−En=QT(n)+QR(n).\begin{aligned} Q_T(n)&=-\Delta\langle H_T\rangle_n,\\ Q_R(n)&=-\Delta\langle H_R\rangle_n,\\ E_{n+1}-E_n&=Q_T(n)+Q_R(n). \end{aligned}(6.11)

In this cycle, coherent round trips and free evolution contribute no net system energy change [1]. Any additional driving or leakage in a physical realization requires the corresponding energy flows to be included. Thermal-exchange and restoration outputs can be read stage by stage in independent repetitions with the same preparation, avoiding changes to the original cycle from additional intermediate measurements.

The cooling curve of Chapter 4 can be tested in the same way. Use its zero-temperature environment and restoration to the zero-energy background, so positive-energy modes can only exit and have the same exit share ϵ>0\epsilon>0. Starting from the state after one completed cooling cycle, with initial mean energy Einit>0E_{\mathrm{init}}>0,

En=Einit(1−ϵ)n,ΓE=−log⁡(1−ϵ)τtot,TE(t)∼ΔΓEt,Δ=log⁡p.\begin{aligned} E_n&=E_{\mathrm{init}}(1-\epsilon)^n,\\ \Gamma_E&=-\frac{\log(1-\epsilon)}{\tau_{\mathrm{tot}}},\\ T_E(t)&\sim\frac{\Delta}{\Gamma_Et},\qquad \Delta=\log p. \end{aligned}(6.12)

After determining ϵ\epsilon from single-cycle exchange, compare the predicted energy curve with system and environment energy readings. The quantity TET_E is obtained from this energy through the full partition function.

Entropy adds a constraint beyond energy. Return to a fixed finite positive temperature with same-temperature restoration, reconstruct the system density operator from repeated trials with the same preparation, and compare it with the two independently measured energy flows:

Σn=S(ρn+1)−S(ρn)−β[QT(n)+QR(n)]=Dn−Dn+1≥0.\begin{aligned} \Sigma_n &=S(\rho_{n+1})-S(\rho_n)\\ &\quad-\beta[Q_T(n)+Q_R(n)]\\ &=D_n-D_{n+1}\ge0. \end{aligned}(6.13)

For preparations that remain diagonal, all mode probabilities determine the system entropy. When coherence is present, off-diagonal structure must be included. Entropy calculated only from total energy-shell shares is generally insufficient to test this relation.

With the pure restoration preparation of Section 5.3, readings of the restoration outputs also test the preparation change and complete balance:

CR=S(ηR′)+βQR,Σn+CR=IT+D(ηT′‖ηT)+IR.\begin{aligned} C_R&=S(\eta_R')+\beta Q_R,\\ \Sigma_n+C_R &=I_T+D(\eta_T'\Vert\eta_T)+I_R. \end{aligned}(6.14)

These quantities must be determined from the joint system–auxiliary states at their respective stages.

For the driven cycle of Section 3.6, measurements of maintenance energy together with the switching envelopes determine the control work, and the complete-cycle spectrum determines relaxation. With system energy measured by HK+MH_K+M at both endpoints, the system and environment energy changes must sum to WctrlW_{\mathrm{ctrl}}.

6.4 Environment Refreshing and Return

The preceding multi-cycle predictions use independent fresh environments. To test this condition, keep the single-cycle joint action fixed but retain and reintroduce the same thermal environment and restoration auxiliary, preserving their correlations between cycles. The next input is then generally no longer a product of the system and a prescribed fresh environment, so the full joint state must be propagated [27]. Effects of environmental correlations on successive collisions have been studied in specific collision models and their optical simulations [28,29].

Independence concerns the complete joint input, ρSOEnew=ρSO⊗ηfull\rho_{SOE_{\mathrm{new}}}=\rho_{SO}\otimes\eta_{\mathrm{full}}, where OO includes the shared source and old outputs. A formation source that retains distinctions between earlier outputs may correlate later resources with the system even when each resource has the same thermal marginal.

A finite environment can also realize the fresh-auxiliary arrangement for a finite observation time. Prepare NN mutually independent sets of complete auxiliaries, also independent of the initial system, each in the prescribed ηfull\eta_{\mathrm{full}}. Use one set per cycle, with old outputs no longer participating and unused auxiliaries left undisturbed. The first NN cycles then give exactly ρn=ℱn(ρ0)\rho_n=\mathcal F^n(\rho_0). Beyond this supply window, preparation and return conditions must be reconsidered. The comparison below instead retains the same auxiliaries from the first cycle onward.

This comparison requires the complete unitary action to be fixed, including its action on returning restoration outputs. Reusing the reference apparatus of Section 2.5 likewise requires specifying its action on used inputs. Equality of the system channels for fresh inputs does not guarantee identical return curves for old outputs. We use the restoration rotation of the established cycle [1]:

Ures=exp⁡[π2(L−L†)],L=∑b|Yb⟩⟨eb,g|,|Yb⟩=∑aga|ea,rab⟩.\begin{aligned} U_{\mathrm{res}}&=\exp\!\left[\frac{\pi}{2}(L-L^\dagger)\right],\\ L&=\sum_b|Y_b\rangle\langle e_b,g|,\\ |Y_b\rangle&=\sum_a\sqrt{g_a}|e_a,r_{ab}\rangle. \end{aligned}(6.15)

Here |g⟩|g\rangle is the initial restoration-auxiliary label and |rab⟩|r_{ab}\rangle are its orthogonal output labels. For the zero-temperature preparation ga=δa0g_a=\delta_{a0}, we have |Yb⟩=|e0,r0b⟩|Y_b\rangle=|e_0,r_{0b}\rangle. This rotation specifies forward restoration, output return, and the action on the orthogonal complement.

Prepare the system initially in a positive-energy matter mode |ν⟩|\nu\rangle that exchanges only with e0e_0, with channel weight aa and exchange angle α\alpha. At zero temperature, the thermal input for this channel is |u⟩|u\rangle. The interaction-picture retrieval phase is wν=ei(φν+τtotEν)w_\nu=e^{i(\varphi_\nu+\tau_{\mathrm{tot}}E_\nu)}; together with the free phase it gives the net cycle phase of Chapter 3. Choose wν=1w_\nu=1 for this example; other directions need not have the same phase. In the order system, thermal environment, restoration auxiliary, define

|A⟩=|ν,u,g⟩,|B⟩=|e0,v,g⟩,|C⟩=|e0,v,r00⟩,|D⟩=|ν,u,r00⟩.\begin{aligned} |A\rangle&=|\nu,u,g\rangle,& |B\rangle&=|e_0,v,g\rangle,\\ |C\rangle&=|e_0,v,r_{00}\rangle,& |D\rangle&=|\nu,u,r_{00}\rangle. \end{aligned}(6.16)

These four states span an invariant sector of the complete joint action. The coherent round trip within a stage still passes through intermediate states and returns to this sector after full retrieval. Thermal exchange rotates the pairs (A,B)(A,B) and (D,C)(D,C), while restoration gives B↦CB\mapsto C and C↦−BC\mapsto-B. All four states have the same total energy. Removing the common free phase and writing cα=cos⁡αc_\alpha=\cos\alpha, sα=sin⁡αs_\alpha=\sin\alpha, the single-cycle action is

U4=(cα−sα0000−cα−sαsαcα0000−sαcα).U_4= \begin{pmatrix} c_\alpha&-s_\alpha&0&0\\ 0&0&-c_\alpha&-s_\alpha\\ s_\alpha&c_\alpha&0&0\\ 0&0&-s_\alpha&c_\alpha \end{pmatrix}.(6.17)

When all auxiliaries are refreshed each cycle, the system encounters this channel with share aa each time. Once the positive-energy mode exits, it cannot be reformed by a zero-temperature environment. Its occupation is therefore

Pνnew(n)=(1−asin⁡2α)n.P_\nu^{\mathrm{new}}(n) =(1-a\sin^2\alpha)^n.(6.18)

When the same auxiliaries are retained, the initial share 1−a1-a in other orthogonal thermal blocks never exchanges with this mode. The share aa in the selected block evolves repeatedly within the four-state sector. Setting vn=U4n|A⟩v_n=U_4^n|A\rangle gives

qν(n)=|⟨A|vn⟩|2+|⟨D|vn⟩|2,Pνret(n)=1−a+aqν(n).\begin{aligned} q_\nu(n)&=|\langle A|v_n\rangle|^2+|\langle D|v_n\rangle|^2,\\ P_\nu^{\mathrm{ret}}(n)&=1-a+aq_\nu(n). \end{aligned}(6.19)

The first cycle is identical in both processes. In the second cycle, the four-state action gives conditional occupation cos⁡4α+sin⁡4α\cos^4\alpha+\sin^4\alpha of ν\nu, and hence

Pνret(2)−Pνnew(2)=a(2−a)sin⁡4α>0.P_\nu^{\mathrm{ret}}(2)-P_\nu^{\mathrm{new}}(2) =a(2-a)\sin^4\alpha>0.(6.20)

The difference is produced by reusing the same outputs. For a=0.4a=0.4 and α=0.8\alpha=0.8, the first three occupations with refreshed auxiliaries are approximately 0.7942,0.6307,0.50090.7942,0.6307,0.5009; with retained auxiliaries, they are 0.7942,0.8002,0.99980.7942,0.8002,0.9998, already showing pronounced return.

More general return phases, finite temperatures, and auxiliary structures change the return curve and require the corresponding complete unitary action to be calculated. Absence of visible return during a finite observation time does not establish that the environment never returns.

7. Conclusion

Thermal equilibrium is established through sustained exchange between matter and the environment. Matter exit, renewed formation, and background restoration jointly change the overall occupations, while coherence evolves with distinctions in the full joint outputs. The complete cycle determines the equilibrium distribution, relaxation modes, and information balance of the system and environment together.

For the same-temperature cycle on a finite state space, under the independent-refreshing conditions of Chapter 2, finite positive temperature, preparation weight a0>0a_0>0 for no thermal exchange, and exit share ϵν>0\epsilon_\nu>0 for every matter mode, any initial state converges to the unique full thermal state:

ℱπn(ρ0)→ρβ,ρβ=e−βHKZK,ZK=∑j=0K|Sj|e−βEj.\begin{aligned} \mathcal F_\pi^{\,n}(\rho_0)&\longrightarrow\rho_\beta,\\ \rho_\beta&=\frac{e^{-\beta H_K}}{Z_K},\\ Z_K&=\sum_{j=0}^{K}|S_j|e^{-\beta E_j}. \end{aligned}(7.1)

Convergence to this state includes relaxation of the energy distribution, composition within shells, and coherence. Shell degeneracies and restoration preparation jointly determine equilibrium occupations, while microscopic forward and reverse exchanges may continue after statistical balance is established.

For the propagation used here, which does not mix matter modes, the nonequilibrium modes of the same cycle determine the relaxation rates. After the first background restoration, a nonzero decay factor λr\lambda_r corresponds to the physical-time rate

Γr=−log⁡|λr|τtot,0<|λr|<1.\Gamma_r=-\frac{\log|\lambda_r|}{\tau_{\mathrm{tot}}}, \qquad 0<|\lambda_r|<1.(7.2)

Occupations and coherences can decay at different rates. Actual readings also depend on which modes the initial state excites and which components the observable can access. Internal composition can continue changing after mean energy has approached equilibrium. Under weak exchange, removing the net cycle phase on the restored family of states yields continuous relaxation equations from the slow-time limit of the same cycle, with errors controlled over finite slow times. Exact cycle factors and continuous rates thus have a common dynamical origin.

Target exchange on complete carriers and a same-temperature reference provide a concrete physical realization of the thermal cycle. Under the encoded-subspace preservation and shell-energy commutation conditions of Section 3.6, finite switching incorporates maintenance into the cycle: control work balances changes in activity energy, the shell Gibbs state remains the unique attracting state, and relaxation is governed by the complete driven-cycle spectrum.

Cooling is read through changes in shell energy HKH_K, to which both thermal exchange and background restoration contribute:

En+1−En=QT(n)+QR(n).E_{n+1}-E_n=Q_T(n)+Q_R(n).(7.3)

As the environment temperature changes, thermal-state tracking is determined by the competition between target-distribution motion and internal relaxation. For the specified zero-temperature exit process with fixed cycle parameters, nonzero energy decays exponentially according to the slow mode. Temperature calibrated from the full finite spectrum satisfies TE∼Δ/(ΓEt)T_E\sim\Delta/(\Gamma_Et) at late times, where Δ=log⁡p\Delta=\log p is the first excitation gap. This temperature reading characterizes mean energy; complete thermalization also includes relaxation of internal composition and coherence.

The time direction of thermalization is linked to the fate of the outputs. Returning to fixed finite positive temperature and same-temperature restoration, the decrease in deviation from the thermal state gives the relaxation entropy production. Including the change in the actual pure restoration preparation yields

Σn=Dn−Dn+1=ΔSS−β(QT+QR)≥0,Σn+CR=IT+D(ηT′‖ηT)+IR.\begin{aligned} \Sigma_n&=D_n-D_{n+1}\\ &=\Delta S_S-\beta(Q_T+Q_R)\ge0,\\ \Sigma_n+C_R &=I_T+D(\eta_T'\Vert\eta_T)+I_R. \end{aligned}(7.4)

At system equilibrium, Σn=0\Sigma_n=0, while restoration auxiliaries may still develop correlations and change preparation. System relaxation entropy production and changes in environment preparation are therefore distinct contributions to the same joint balance.

Retaining the complete final joint state and its correlations and applying the inverse joint unitaries in reverse order still recovers the initial state. Gradual loss of initial-state memory in the system is compatible with reversible joint evolution. If old auxiliaries participate again, subsequent exchange must be calculated from the actual joint state and its correlations. The complete action specified in the main text gives a return curve distinct from the fresh-auxiliary process.

Once channel weights, exchange angles, environment preparations, and total elapsed duration are independently fixed, equilibrium occupations, internal composition, coherence envelopes, and energy outputs must satisfy the same set of predictions. Changing how auxiliaries return further tests the role of environmental conditions. The endpoint, rate, and time direction of thermalization are thereby mutually constrained results of one dynamical process.

Computations and Data

The results are obtained through analytical derivations and finite-dimensional numerical checks; no experimental data are used. Curves are calculated with the preparations, channels, and initial states specified in their captions, while schematic diagrams do not represent numerical results. The accompanying programs check the complete quantum channel, relaxation spectrum, weak-exchange slow-time limit, thermal-state tracking under changing temperature, cooling corrections, energy and entropy balances, and joint evolution with fresh or returning auxiliaries. Further matrix checks cover complete-carrier exchange, same-temperature reference restoration, and the driven cycle during maintenance, testing energy conservation, actual auxiliary outputs, control work, and the complete-cycle spectrum. Numerical checks verify the implementation of formulas and figures. The scope of the analytical conclusions is determined by the conditions in the main text.
